varmland.t: Forested petty kingdom north of Lake Vänern, known mostly from the Norse sagas, later absorbed into the Swedish realm.
varmland.o: Värmland, the land around the rivers flowing into Lake Vänern, is known mainly from Icelandic sagas written centuries later. [[e:snorri-sturluson|Snorri Sturluson's]] Ynglinga saga tells that Olof the Tree-Feller, driven from Uppsala, cleared the forests here and founded a new line of kings.
varmland.r: Its people lived by farming, iron extraction from bog ore and forest trades, and met at their own assemblies. The sagas describe Värmland as a borderland contested by Norwegian, Svear and Geatish kings, with local kings or jarls of uncertain historical reality.
varmland.e: By around 1000 Värmland was drawn into the orbit of the Swedish kings, although Norwegian rulers such as [[e:olaf-ii-of-norway|Olaf Haraldsson]] also tried to claim it. It became a province of the [[s:kingdom-of-sweden|Kingdom of Sweden]], keeping its own law and lawman in the [[e:middle-ages|Middle Ages]].

vulci.t: Wealthy Etruscan city near the Fiora river whose tombs held thousands of Greek vases and whose François Tomb preserves an Etruscan version of early Roman history.
vulci.o: Vulci, Etruscan Velch, grew from Villanovan villages on a plateau above the Fiora river, some 10 km from the coast. By the 7th and 6th centuries BCE it had become one of the richest cities of Etruria, importing luxury goods and controlling a large territory reaching towards [[e:lake-bolsena|Lake Bolsena]].
vulci.r: Vulci was a major centre of [[e:bronze-working|bronze-working]], exporting tripods, vessels and candelabra across [[e:italy|Italy]] and beyond the [[e:alps|Alps]]. Its tombs yielded an extraordinary number of Athenian painted vases, many excavated by Lucien Bonaparte in the 19th century. The François Tomb's paintings show the Vulcian heroes Caile and Avle Vipinas and Macstrna, whom the emperor Claudius identified with [[e:rome|Rome's]] king [[e:servius-tullius|Servius Tullius]].
vulci.e: [[e:rome|Rome]] defeated Vulci together with [[s:volsinii|Volsinii]] in 280 BCE, when Tiberius Coruncanius celebrated a triumph over both. Much of its coastal land was confiscated and the [[e:latin|Latin]] colony of Cosa founded there in 273 BCE. The city declined into a minor Roman town and was abandoned in the early [[e:middle-ages|Middle Ages]].

vasates.t: Aquitanian people south of the Garonne whose town Cossium became Bazas, centre of the Bazadais.
vasates.o: The Vasates, called Vocates by Caesar, lived south of the middle Garonne in the modern Gironde. They surrendered to [[e:publius-licinius-crassus|Publius Crassus]] in 56 BCE with the other Aquitanian peoples.
vasates.r: No rulers or institutions are known. Their territory lay between the Garonne valley and the Landes forest, on the route from Burdigala to the [[e:pyrenees|Pyrenees]].
vasates.e: Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their chief town Cossium was renamed Civitas Vasatica, from which comes Bazas. The poet Ausonius had family links with the town, and its district kept the name Bazadais.

venetian-cyprus.t: Cyprus under the Republic of Venice from 1489 to 1571, a heavily fortified frontier colony lost to the Ottomans in a famous siege of Famagusta.
venetian-cyprus.o: Venetian influence in the [[s:kingdom-of-cyprus|Kingdom of Cyprus]] grew through the marriage of King James II to the Venetian [[e:catherine-cornaro|Catherine Cornaro]]. After his death and that of their infant son, [[e:venice|Venice]] controlled Catherine's government, and in 1489 forced her to abdicate and cede the island to the Republic.
venetian-cyprus.r: A Venetian lieutenant and councillors ruled from Nicosia, keeping the old Frankish nobility while taxing heavily. [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]] exported [[e:cotton|cotton]], [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], salt and wine, and paid tribute to [[e:mamluk-sultanate|Mamluk Egypt]] and later the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]]. Fearing invasion, [[e:venice|Venice]] rebuilt the walls of [[s:genoese-famagusta|Famagusta]] and in 1567 built new star-shaped bastions around Nicosia.
venetian-cyprus.e: The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] invaded in 1570. Nicosia fell in September 1570, and [[s:genoese-famagusta|Famagusta]] surrendered in August 1571 after a long siege; its commander Marco Antonio Bragadin was flayed alive. [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]] became an Ottoman province.

venetian-nauplia.t: Venetian-ruled port of Nauplia, called Napoli di Romania, a fortified base in the Argolid for a century and a half.
venetian-nauplia.o: In 1388 [[e:marie-of-enghien|Marie of Enghien]], heiress of the [[s:lordship-of-argos-and-nauplia|Lordship of Argos and Nauplia]], sold her lands to [[e:venice|Venice]]. The Byzantine despot Theodore I seized [[s:argos|Argos]] first, but returned it to Venice in 1394. Nauplia, which the Venetians called Napoli di [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]], became the centre of Venetian rule in the eastern Peloponnese.
venetian-nauplia.r: Venetian officials governed from Nauplia, strengthening the walls of the Acronauplia and building the harbour fort of Bourtzi in 1471. The town traded grain, wine and [[e:silk|silk]] and hosted Greek, Albanian and Italian communities; Albanian soldiers (stradioti) served [[e:venice|Venice]]. [[s:argos|Argos]] was lost to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in 1463, leaving Nauplia an outpost surrounded by Ottoman territory.
venetian-nauplia.e: After the Ottoman-Venetian war of 1537-1540, [[e:venice|Venice]] surrendered Nauplia and Monemvasia to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] under the peace treaty of 1540. Venice returned in 1686 during the creation of the [[s:venetian-morea|Venetian Morea]].

viscounty-of-bearn.t: Pyrenean lordship that made itself a sovereign state under Gaston Fébus and gave France its king Henry IV.
viscounty-of-bearn.o: Béarn emerged in the 9th century as a viscounty within the [[s:duchy-of-gascony|Duchy of Gascony]], ruled by a family later called the Centulles from Lescar and then Morlaàs. [[e:gaston-iv-of-bearn|Gaston IV]] took part in the [[e:first-crusade|First Crusade]] and helped [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]] conquer [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]] in 1118. The seat later moved to Orthez and, from 1464, to Pau.
viscounty-of-bearn.r: The Fors de Béarn guaranteed local liberties, and the viscount had to swear to respect them. Gaston III, called Fébus, refused homage to both [[e:france|France]] and [[e:england|England]] in 1347 and ruled Béarn as a sovereign land; he also wrote a famous treatise on hunting. Through marriages the viscounts became counts of Foix and kings of [[e:kingdom-of-navarre|Navarre]].
viscounty-of-bearn.e: [[e:jeanne-dalbret|Queen Jeanne d'Albret]] made [[e:calvinism|Calvinism]] the official religion in the 1560s. Her son Henry, born at Pau, became [[e:henry-iv-of-france|Henry IV of France]] in 1589, but Béarn stayed separate until [[e:louis-xiii-of-france|Louis XIII]] annexed it in 1620 and restored [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]].

venetian-morea.t: The Peloponnese under Venice after Morosini's conquest in 1685-1687, a brief reform-minded colony that collapsed in the Ottoman reconquest of 1715.
venetian-morea.o: In the Morean War, part of the [[e:great-turkish-war|Great Turkish War]], the Venetian commander [[e:francesco-morosini|Francesco Morosini]] conquered the Peloponnese between 1685 and 1687; during his campaign in Attica a Venetian shell exploded the Parthenon. The [[e:treaty-of-karlowitz|Treaty of Karlowitz]] in 1699 confirmed Venetian possession of the Morea as the Kingdom of the Morea.
venetian-morea.r: [[e:venice|Venice]] divided the peninsula into four provinces under a provveditore generale at Nauplia, carried out a detailed [[e:census|census]] and land register, and settled colonists to revive a depopulated, war-damaged land. It favoured the Catholic church, which irritated the [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] majority, and built the great fortress of Palamidi above Nauplia in 1711-1714.
venetian-morea.e: The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] attacked in 1715 and took the whole Morea within a few months, helped by weak garrisons and the indifference of the [[e:greeks|Greeks]]. The Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 confirmed the Ottoman reconquest.

venetian-modon-and-coron.t: Twin Venetian fortress ports at the south-western tip of the Peloponnese, known as the eyes of the Republic, which guarded Venice's route to the Levant for three centuries.
venetian-modon-and-coron.o: [[e:venice|Venice]] claimed the south-western Peloponnese in the partition of the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]] after 1204. Venetian forces occupied Modon (Methoni) and Coron (Koroni) around 1207, and the Treaty of Sapienza with Geoffrey I of Villehardouin of the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]] confirmed them in 1209.
venetian-modon-and-coron.r: The two ports were governed by Venetian castellans and officials appointed from [[e:venice|Venice]], and served as stopovers for merchant [[e:galley|galleys]] and pilgrim ships bound for the [[e:holy-land|Holy Land]] and the eastern [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]]. Their surroundings produced wine, [[e:silk|silk]] and food for the fleets, and they gathered news about the [[e:aegean|Aegean]], hence their nickname. Greek, Jewish and Albanian communities lived under Venetian rule.
venetian-modon-and-coron.e: In 1500, during the Ottoman-Venetian war, [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Bayezid II stormed Modon after a long siege, and Coron surrendered soon after. [[e:venice|Venice]] briefly regained them in 1686-1715 as part of the [[s:venetian-morea|Venetian Morea]]. The fortress of Methoni still stands.

varman-dynasty-of-bengal.t: A dynasty of eastern Bengal ruling from Vikramapura in the late 11th and early 12th centuries, between the Chandras and the Senas.
varman-dynasty-of-bengal.o: The Varmans claimed descent from a Yadava family of Simhapura, probably in [[s:kingdom-of-kalinga|Kalinga]]. Jatavarman, who married a princess of the [[s:kalachuris-of-tripuri|Kalachuris of Tripuri]], established their rule in Vanga as the [[s:pala-empire|Pala Empire]] weakened in the late 11th century, after the fall of the [[s:chandra-dynasty|Chandra dynasty]].
varman-dynasty-of-bengal.r: The Varmans ruled from Vikramapura near Dhaka and were patrons of [[e:brahmanism|Brahmanical Hinduism]]. Harivarman's minister Bhavadeva Bhatta was a noted scholar of Vedic ritual and law. The dynasty is known from a small number of [[e:copper|copper]] plates, such as the Belava plate of Bhojavarman, and from Bhavadeva's inscription.
varman-dynasty-of-bengal.e: In the early 12th century Vijayasena of the [[s:sena-dynasty|Sena dynasty]] took eastern [[e:bengal|Bengal]], ending Varman rule.

viye-kingdom.t: An Ovimbundu kingdom of the Bie plateau whose traders carried goods across Central Africa, and whose defeat in 1890 opened the interior to Portugal.
viye-kingdom.o: Viye (Bie) was founded by the 18th century, tradition says by a hunter named Viye, on the eastern edge of the Angolan central highlands. Like the [[s:bailundo-kingdom|Bailundo Kingdom]], it grew as a raiding and trading state supplying captives to Benguela.
viye-kingdom.r: Viye's kings ruled from a fortified capital through titled officials. [[e:ovimbundu|Ovimbundu]] caravans from Viye travelled to the [[e:lunda-empire|Lunda]] lands, the upper [[e:zambezi|Zambezi]] and Katanga, trading in slaves, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], beeswax and later [[e:rubber|rubber]]. The Portuguese trader Antonio da Silva Porto lived at Belmonte in Viye for decades and led trading expeditions into the interior.
viye-kingdom.e: In 1890 King Ndunduma expelled a Portuguese expedition, and Silva Porto died after the confrontation. Portugal sent a punitive force that defeated Ndunduma and exiled him, bringing Viye into [[s:portuguese-angola|Portuguese Angola]]. The town of Kuito grew on its lands.

veii.t: The richest Etruscan city near Rome, its great rival for three centuries until Marcus Furius Camillus captured it in 396 BCE after a ten-year siege.
veii.o: Veii stood on a defended tufa plateau about 16 km north of [[e:rome|Rome]], and grew from several Villanovan villages that merged into one large settlement by the 8th century BCE. It controlled the right bank of the [[e:tiber-river|Tiber]] and the salt and trade routes that Rome also wanted, making conflict between the two almost inevitable.
veii.r: Veii was famed for its craftsmen: the terracotta statues of the Portonaccio temple, including the Apollo of Veii, are among the finest Etruscan works, and Roman tradition credited a Veientine sculptor, Vulca, with the cult statue of Jupiter on the Capitol. Its territory had dense rural settlement and a sophisticated system of drainage tunnels. It was ruled by kings, notably [[e:lars-tolumnius|Lars Tolumnius]] in the late 5th century.
veii.e: [[e:rome|Rome]] and Veii fought repeatedly over [[s:fidenae|Fidenae]] and the [[e:tiber-river|Tiber]] crossing. In 396 BCE, after a siege said to have lasted ten years, Camillus took the city, reportedly by tunnelling under its walls. Its land was divided among Roman citizens, doubling Rome's territory, and the city never recovered as an independent power.

viscounty-of-narbonne.t: The viscounty of the old Roman port of Narbonne, famed under Viscountess Ermengard as a centre of troubadour culture and Mediterranean trade.
viscounty-of-narbonne.o: Viscounts appear at Narbonne around 900 as deputies of the counts of [[s:county-of-toulouse|Toulouse]], who had inherited authority over the former Carolingian march of Septimania. The office became hereditary, and the viscounts shared power in the city with its powerful archbishops.
viscounty-of-narbonne.r: Narbonne was a busy port and a centre of Jewish learning. Viscountess Ermengard, who ruled from 1134 to 1192, presided over a court celebrated by troubadours and steered between [[s:county-of-toulouse|Toulouse]] and Barcelona. Later viscounts survived the [[e:albigensian-crusade|Albigensian Crusade]] by siding with the crusaders, while the river's shift and the silting of the port slowly cut the city's trade.
viscounty-of-narbonne.e: The viscounty passed to the house of Foix in the 15th century. In 1507 Gaston de Foix exchanged it with his uncle [[e:louis-xii-of-france|Louis XII]] for the duchy of Nemours, and it was joined to the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].
ru: Gaston de Foix, Duke of Nemours

vishnukundina-dynasty.t: A Deccan dynasty of the Krishna-Godavari region that ruled coastal Andhra and Telangana before the rise of the Eastern Chalukyas.
vishnukundina-dynasty.o: The Vishnukundinas emerged in the 5th century, possibly in Telangana, and expanded towards the coast, taking Vengi from the [[s:salankayana-dynasty|Salankayana dynasty]]. Their capitals included Indrapalanagara, Amarapura and Denduluru. They became the main power of the eastern [[e:deccan|Deccan]] after the decline of the [[s:vakataka-dynasty|Vakataka dynasty]], with whom they had marriage ties.
vishnukundina-dynasty.r: Kings such as [[e:madhavavarma-ii|Madhavavarma II]], who performed horse sacrifices, presented themselves as Vedic rulers, though they also supported Buddhist monasteries. Their [[e:copper|copper]]-plate charters in [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] record land grants to [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]]. The rock-cut cave temples at Undavalli and Mogalrajapuram near Vijayawada are attributed to their period.
vishnukundina-dynasty.e: In the early 7th century [[e:pulakeshin-ii|Pulakeshin II]] of the [[s:chalukyas-of-badami|Chalukyas of Badami]] conquered the Vengi region and gave it to his brother [[e:kubja-vishnuvardhana|Kubja Vishnuvardhana]], who founded the [[s:eastern-chalukyas|Eastern Chalukyas]] around 624.

volcae-arecomici.t: Celtic people of eastern Languedoc whose sacred spring at Nemausus became the Roman city of Nîmes.
volcae-arecomici.o: The Arecomici were the eastern branch of the Volcae, a Celtic people who settled between the Rhône and the Hérault in the 3rd century BCE. Strabo records that twenty-four villages were subject to their chief town Nemausus, which grew up around a sacred spring.
volcae-arecomici.r: They lived in hilltop oppida such as Nages, and Nemausus had a stone tower, the Tour Magne, before the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] arrived. They traded closely with [[s:massalia|Massalia]] and struck coins with Greek and [[e:latin|Latin]] letters.
volcae-arecomici.e: Their land came under [[e:rome|Rome]] in 121 BCE and part of it was given to [[s:massalia|Massalia]] by [[e:pompey|Pompey]]. Nemausus became a [[e:latin|Latin]] colony with rich monuments, including the Maison Carrée and the aqueduct carried by the Pont du Gard.

volsinii.t: Leading Etruscan city whose shrine of Voltumna was the religious heart of the Etruscan League, crushed by Rome in 264 BCE after a slave uprising.
volsinii.o: Volsinii, Etruscan [[s:felsina|Velzna]], grew on the volcanic plateau of modern [[s:commune-of-orvieto|Orvieto]] from Villanovan settlements of the early 1st millennium BCE. By the 6th century BCE it was a wealthy city with orderly necropolises such as Crocifisso del Tufo, where tombs were laid out in streets and inscribed with owners' names.
volsinii.r: Volsinii controlled a rich territory around [[e:lake-bolsena|Lake Bolsena]] and traded widely, as imported Greek pottery shows. Nearby lay the [[e:fanum-voltumnae|Fanum Voltumnae]], the federal sanctuary where the twelve Etruscan peoples met each year for games, cult and council. The city was governed by an aristocracy; ancient sources say it was so rich that [[e:rome|Rome]] took some 2,000 statues as booty from it.
volsinii.e: After wars with [[e:rome|Rome]] in the 4th and early 3rd centuries, Volsinii's aristocrats asked Rome for help when [[e:freedmen|freedmen]] and former slaves seized power. Rome besieged and destroyed the city in 264 BCE and moved survivors to Volsinii Novi, modern Bolsena. Rome also transferred the cult of Vertumnus to the Aventine.

videha.t: A Later Vedic kingdom in Mithila, north of the Ganges, famed for the philosopher-king Janaka and the debates that shaped the Upanishads.
videha.o: The Shatapatha Brahmana tells how Videgha Mathava, guided by the fire god Agni, carried Vedic culture east across the Sadanira river, probably the Gandak, into the marshy lands of Mithila. The kingdom that grew there lay in what is now northern Bihar and the Terai of [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Nepal]], and it was one of the easternmost Vedic states.
videha.r: Videha's court became a centre of speculative thought. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad King Janaka hosts contests between [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] teachers, and the sage Yajnavalkya expounds the doctrine of the self, atman, and its identity with brahman. Wealth came from [[e:rice|rice]] grown on the fertile floodplain. Later epic tradition made Sita, heroine of the Ramayana, the daughter of a Janaka of Videha.
videha.e: By around 600 BCE the monarchy had given way to a republican order, and the Videhas became members of the [[s:vajji|Vajji]] confederacy centred on [[e:vaishali|Vaishali]]. [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]] conquered the confederacy in the 5th century BCE. The name Mithila survives for the region, and its people still speak Maithili.

vijaynagar-state.t: A small Rajput state in the forested hills of northern Gujarat, also known as Pol, on the borderlands with Rajasthan.
vijaynagar-state.o: The state took its earlier name from Pol, a hill town among the Aravalli spurs of the [[e:mahi-kantha-agency|Mahi Kantha]] region. Its [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] rulers held this frontier zone from the later 16th century, though the details of its founding are poorly recorded.
vijaynagar-state.r: The ruler, styled Rao, governed a sparsely settled tract of hills and forest with a large Bhil population. In the British period the state was grouped in the [[e:mahi-kantha-agency|Mahi Kantha Agency]]. The area is known for its ruined temples at Polo, deep in the forest near the old capital.
vijaynagar-state.e: In 1948 the state was merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]], and its territory became part of Sabarkantha district when [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] was formed in 1960. The Polo forest is now a protected area.

volsci.t: Italic people of southern Latium who raided and fought Rome for two centuries, the enemies of the legendary Coriolanus.
volsci.o: The Volsci spoke an Osco-Umbrian language and appear in the late 6th century BCE moving from the Apennines into the Lepini mountains, the Liri valley and the Pontine plain. They took over existing [[e:latin|Latin]] towns such as Velitrae, Satricum and Antium, and Anxur (Tarracina) on the coast.
volsci.r: The Volsci formed a loose group of towns rather than a unified state, cooperating in war, often alongside the [[s:aequi|Aequi]]. Antium was a port with a fleet that raided the coast. Their language is known chiefly from a bronze tablet from Velitrae. Roman legend made them the people among whom the exiled Gnaeus Marcius Coriolanus took refuge before leading them against [[e:rome|Rome]].
volsci.e: Wars with [[e:rome|Rome]] and the [[e:latins|Latins]] continued through the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. After the [[e:latin-war|Latin War]] Rome took Antium in 338 BCE and displayed the beaks (rostra) of its warships in the Forum. Privernum fell in 329 BCE and Sora in the following decades, and by about 304 BCE the Volsci had been absorbed.

vithalgadh-state.t: A minor chiefship of the Jhalawad country of northern Kathiawar.
vithalgadh-state.o: Vithalgadh was a small estate in the Jhalawad region of Kathiawar, held by a local chiefly family from around 1700. Its founding is poorly documented.
vithalgadh-state.r: The ruler held a few villages and, after 1807, came under British supervision in the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]] as a minor non-salute state. Standard references record little else.
vithalgadh-state.e: Vithalgadh merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in Surendranagar district.

vala-state.t: A small Gohil Rajput state in eastern Kathiawar whose capital stood on the ruins of Valabhi, the great early medieval city of the Maitrakas.
vala-state.o: Vala was founded around 1740 by a junior branch of the [[e:gohil|Gohil Rajputs]] who ruled [[s:bhavnagar-state|Bhavnagar State]]. Its town, Vala or Vallabhipur, lay at the site of ancient Valabhi, capital of the Maitraka kingdom and a renowned Buddhist and Jain centre of learning.
vala-state.r: The Thakor ruled a modest agricultural territory within the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]]. Few details of the state's internal history are recorded; the site is better known for the excavations and inscriptions of ancient Valabhi than for its 18th and 19th century rulers.
vala-state.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]] Vala was merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948; it now lies in [[s:bhavnagar-state|Bhavnagar]] district of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

veronese-league.t: A short-lived alliance of Veneto cities against Frederick Barbarossa's officials, and the forerunner of the Lombard League.
veronese-league.o: In 1164 [[s:commune-of-verona|Verona]], [[s:commune-of-vicenza|Vicenza]], [[s:commune-of-padua|Padua]] and [[s:commune-of-treviso|Treviso]], with the backing of the [[s:republic-of-venice|Republic of Venice]] and the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]], formed a league to resist the taxes and officials imposed by [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Emperor Frederick Barbarossa]] in northern [[e:italy|Italy]].
veronese-league.r: The league was a sworn alliance of independent communes rather than a state. Its members promised mutual defence and refused imperial demands, and Barbarossa failed to subdue them in 1164. [[e:venice|Venice]] supplied money and diplomatic support, eager to keep the emperor out of the Adriatic hinterland.
veronese-league.e: In 1167 the Veronese League merged with the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] cities to form the much larger [[s:lombard-league|Lombard League]], which defeated Barbarossa at [[e:battle-of-legnano|Legnano]] in 1176.

vijayanagara-empire.t: The great south Indian empire whose capital at Hampi was among the largest cities of the 15th and 16th centuries.
vijayanagara-empire.o: Harihara I and his brother Bukka I of the Sangama family founded the kingdom around 1336 on the Tungabhadra river, in territory recently disrupted by the [[e:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate's]] campaigns against the [[s:hoysala-empire|Hoysalas]] and the Kampili kingdom. Tradition credits the sage Vidyaranya with guiding them. The new state quickly absorbed the [[e:hoysala-empire|Hoysala]] lands and the [[s:madurai-sultanate|Madurai Sultanate]].
vijayanagara-empire.r: Four dynasties ruled in turn: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu. Krishnadevaraya, the greatest Tuluva king, defeated the [[s:gajapati-kingdom|Gajapati Kingdom]] and the [[e:deccan-sultanates|Deccan sultanates]] and patronised Telugu and Kannada poets. Nayaka governors held land in return for troops. Foreign visitors such as Abdur Razzaq and Domingo Paes described Hampi's markets, temples and the horse trade with [[s:portuguese-india|Portuguese India]].
vijayanagara-empire.e: A coalition of the [[e:deccan-sultanates|Deccan sultanates]] defeated Vijayanagara at the Battle of Talikota in 1565 and sacked Hampi. The Aravidu kings continued at Penukonda and Chandragiri, but their Nayaka governors in [[e:madurai|Madurai]], Thanjavur, Gingee and Mysore became independent; the last ruler lost his remaining lands by 1646.

varman-dynasty-of-kannauj.t: The kingdom of Yashovarman, who restored Kannauj's power in the 8th century and patronised the poets Bhavabhuti and Vakpatiraja.
varman-dynasty-of-kannauj.o: After the collapse of the [[s:pushyabhuti-dynasty|Pushyabhuti dynasty]], Kannauj passed through several hands. In the early 8th century [[e:yashovarman-of-kannauj|Yashovarman]] made it the capital of a powerful kingdom in the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges plain]]. His origins are unknown, and his family is linked by some historians with the [[s:maukharis|Maukharis]].
varman-dynasty-of-kannauj.r: [[e:yashovarman-of-kannauj|Yashovarman]]'s victory over a king of [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]], probably of the [[s:later-guptas|Later Guptas]], is celebrated in the Prakrit poem Gaudavaho by his court poet Vakpatiraja. The great [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] dramatist Bhavabhuti, author of the Uttararamacharita, also lived at his court. In 731 he sent an embassy to [[e:tang-dynasty|Tang China]], possibly seeking allies against the Tibetans and [[e:arabs|Arabs]].
varman-dynasty-of-kannauj.e: [[e:yashovarman-of-kannauj|Yashovarman]] was defeated by [[e:lalitaditya-muktapida|Lalitaditya Muktapida]] of the [[s:karkota-dynasty|Karkota dynasty]], after which Kannauj was weak. His successors are poorly known, and around 770 the [[s:ayudha-dynasty|Ayudha dynasty]] took Kannauj.

vennicnii.t: People of north-west Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, near a headland he called Vennicnium in modern Donegal.
vennicnii.o: The Vennicnii are known only from [[e:geography-ptolemy|Ptolemy's Geography]] of about 150, which places them on the north-western coast of Ireland, with a headland named Vennicnium Promontorium, usually identified with Bloody Foreland or another point on the Donegal coast. His Irish information came from earlier sailors' reports.
vennicnii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or customs. The rugged coastline and uplands of Donegal supported small farming and fishing communities, and later stone forts such as the [[e:grianan-of-aileach|Grianan of Aileach]] show the importance of hilltop centres in the region.
vennicnii.e: No later source mentions the Vennicnii. Donegal later became the territory of the northern [[e:ui-neill|Uí Néill]] dynasties, including the [[e:cenel-conaill|Cenél Conaill]] and the rulers of the [[s:kingdom-of-ailech|Kingdom of Ailech]].

vaghela-dynasty.t: The last Hindu dynasty of Gujarat, ruling from Anahilavada until Alauddin Khalji's conquest at the start of the 14th century.
vaghela-dynasty.o: The Vaghelas were a branch of the [[e:chaulukya-dynasty|Chaulukyas of Gujarat]]. Lavanaprasada and his son Viradhavala, as ministers and generals, held real power under the last Chaulukya kings from the early 13th century. [[e:vigraharaja-iv|Visaladeva]] took the throne at Anahilavada (Patan) around 1244, formally founding the Vaghela dynasty.
vaghela-dynasty.r: The ministers Vastupala and Tejapala, serving Viradhavala, are famous for building Jain temples at [[e:mount-abu|Mount Abu]], notably the Luna Vasahi at Dilwara, and at Girnar and for their patronage of literature. [[e:gujarat|Gujarat's]] ports, notably Cambay, traded across the [[e:arabian-sea|Arabian Sea]]. The kings fought the Paramaras, the [[s:seuna-yadava-dynasty|Seuna Yadava dynasty]] and the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]].
vaghela-dynasty.e: In 1299 [[e:alauddin-khalji|Alauddin Khalji's]] generals [[e:muhammad-bin-tughluq|Ulugh Khan]] and Nusrat Khan invaded [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] and sacked Anahilavada; Karna fled and his queen Kamala Devi was taken to [[e:delhi|Delhi]]. Karna held out in the south until about 1304, when Gujarat became a province of the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]].

vadia-state.t: A small Kathi state in southern Kathiawar, one of the hereditary estates of the clan that gave the peninsula its name.
vadia-state.o: Vadia was held by a branch of Kathi chiefs, who settled in Kathiawar from the later [[e:middle-ages|medieval period]]. The estate near Amreli took shape as a separate holding by around 1600.
vadia-state.r: The Darbar ruled a small territory of farming villages, paying tribute to the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads of Baroda]] and to [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh]]. After 1807 it came under British supervision in the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]]. Few details of its rulers are widely recorded.
vadia-state.e: Vadia merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in present Amreli district.

van-lang.t: The semi-legendary Bronze Age realm of the Hung kings in the Red River delta, honoured in Vietnam as the first Vietnamese state.
van-lang.o: Vietnamese tradition, first written down in medieval works such as the Linh Nam chich quai and the [[s:ly-dynasty|Dai Viet]] su ky toan thu, traces Van Lang to the Hong Bang dynasty founded in 2879 BCE. Historians link it instead to the [[e:dong-son-culture|Dong Son culture]] of the [[e:red-river-asia|Red River]] and Ma River valleys, which flourished from about the 7th century BCE, with its centre at Phong Chau.
van-lang.r: The Hung kings are said to have ruled through lords called Lac hau and Lac tuong over fifteen territories, a picture that suggests a chiefdom or loose confederation rather than a bureaucratic state. Its people grew wet [[e:rice|rice]] and cast the famous [[e:dong-son-culture|Dong Son]] bronze drums, decorated with boats, birds and warriors, which spread across much of [[e:southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]].
van-lang.e: According to tradition, the last Hung king was overthrown in 258 BCE by [[e:an-duong-vuong|Thuc Phan]], who united Van Lang with the [[e:au-viet|Au Viet]] to form [[s:au-lac|Au Lac]]. The Hung kings are still venerated at the temple on Nghia Linh mountain in Phu Tho, and their death anniversary is a national holiday in [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]].

vaccaei.t: A Celtic people of the Douro plains famed for sharing out land and harvests collectively, who resisted Rome until the 1st century BCE.
vaccaei.o: The Vaccaei occupied the middle Douro valley, in modern Valladolid, Palencia, Zamora and Burgos, from about the 4th century BCE. Their towns included Intercatia, Pallantia, Cauca and Pintia.
vaccaei.r: Diodorus records that they divided their land each year by lot, pooled the harvest and gave each family its share, punishing hoarding with death. They lived in large towns on the open cereal plains, and the cemetery of Las Ruedas at Pintia shows a warrior elite. They spoke a Celtic language.
vaccaei.e: [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]] raided them in 220 BCE. In 151 BCE Lucullus massacred the people of Cauca, and later Pallantia withstood several Roman sieges. The Vaccaei fought on into the 1st century BCE, last rising in 56 BCE, before being absorbed into [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]].

venetian-crete.t: Venice's most important overseas colony for over four centuries, where Greek and Italian culture blended to produce El Greco and the Cretan Renaissance.
venetian-crete.o: After the [[e:fourth-crusade|Fourth Crusade]], [[e:venice|Venice]] bought the claim to [[e:crete|Crete]] from [[e:boniface-i-marquis-of-montferrat|Boniface of Montferrat]] in 1204. The Genoese adventurer Enrico Pescatore occupied the island first, and Venice only took control around 1211-1212, sending colonists who received land in return for military service. The capital, Candia, gave its name to the colony.
venetian-crete.r: A Venetian duke and councillors governed, and Venetian settlers formed a feudal nobility over a Greek [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] peasantry whose church was subordinated to [[e:latin|Latin]] [[e:bishop|bishops]]. Frequent revolts, including the [[s:republic-of-saint-titus|Revolt of Saint Titus]] of 1363, were crushed. [[e:crete|Crete]] exported wine (malmsey), oil and grain. In the 16th and early 17th centuries Greek-Italian culture flourished: the Cretan school of icon painting, El Greco and the romance Erotokritos.
venetian-crete.e: The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] invaded in 1645 and besieged Candia for more than twenty years, one of the longest sieges in history. Candia surrendered in 1669, ending Venetian rule except for a few island forts.

vaiga.t: Ancient Estonian district on the western shore of Lake Peipus, contested between Novgorod and the Livonian crusaders.
vaiga.o: Vaiga, called Waiga in [[e:latin|Latin]] sources, lay north of Tartu between the Emajõgi river and [[e:lake-peipus|Lake Peipus]]. It is known from [[e:henry-of-livonia|Henry of Livonia's]] chronicle as one of the smaller Estonian lands of the early 13th century.
vaiga.r: Its people farmed and fished on the lake shore and were exposed to Rus' influence; Novgorod and Pskov raided and levied tribute in the area. Some inhabitants accepted [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] baptism before [[e:latin|Latin]] missionaries arrived. Its elders are not named in the sources.
vaiga.e: Vaiga was conquered by the crusaders in the campaigns of 1220-1224 and became part of the [[s:bishopric-of-dorpat|Bishopric of Dorpat]], on the Livonian border with Pskov and Novgorod.

varduli.t: A people of the western Pyrenean coast in Gipuzkoa and Álava, among the ancestors of the Basques.
varduli.o: The Varduli lived in the area of modern Gipuzkoa and parts of Álava and [[e:kingdom-of-navarre|Navarre]] in the later [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]], between the [[s:caristii|Caristii]] and the [[s:vascones|Vascones]]. Whether they spoke an early form of Basque or a Celtic language is debated.
varduli.r: Little is known of their society. They lived from herding, farming, fishing and the iron of their hills, and Ptolemy names towns such as Gebala and Menosca. Strabo includes them among the rough mountain peoples of the north.
varduli.e: They came under Roman rule as part of the conquest of the north completed in the [[e:cantabrian-wars|Cantabrian Wars]] of 19 BCE, and later supplied [[e:auxilia|auxiliary troops]], including a [[e:cohort|cohort]] of Varduli that served in [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]]. Their land became part of [[s:hispania-tarraconensis|Hispania Tarraconensis]].

vocontii.t: Confederation of the pre-Alps of the Drôme and Vaucluse that became an allied state of Rome, with its towns at Vaison and Die.
vocontii.o: The Vocontii held the mountains and valleys between the Rhône and the [[e:alps|Alps]], from the Drôme to Mont Ventoux. They were a league of smaller communities. [[e:rome|Rome]] campaigned against them under [[e:marcus-fulvius-flaccus-consul-125-bce|Marcus Fulvius Flaccus]] in 124 BCE, during the first wars in Transalpine Gaul.
vocontii.r: After submission they kept unusual autonomy as a federated people, with two capitals, Vasio (Vaison-la-Romaine) and [[e:luc-en-diois|Lucus Augusti]] (Luc-en-Diois), later replaced by Dea Augusta (Die). The historian Pompeius Trogus came from a Vocontian family granted Roman citizenship.
vocontii.e: Their land was incorporated into [[e:gallia-narbonensis|Gallia Narbonensis]]. Vaison-la-Romaine preserves one of the largest excavated Roman towns in [[e:france|France]], with houses, a [[e:theatre|theatre]] and a bridge still in use.

voluntii.t: People of north-east Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, often identified with the Ulaid who gave their name to Ulster.
voluntii.o: The Voluntii, or Uoluntii, appear in [[e:geography-ptolemy|Ptolemy's Geography]] of about 150 on the east coast of Ireland north of the [[s:eblani|Eblani]], in the region of modern Counties Louth and Down. Their name is widely thought to be an early form of [[s:kingdom-of-ulaid|Ulaid]], the people whose name survives in [[s:northern-ireland|Ulster]].
voluntii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or institutions in classical sources. If the identification with the [[s:kingdom-of-ulaid|Ulaid]] is correct, they were the forerunners of the people whose heroic traditions, centred on [[e:emain-macha|Emain Macha]], are preserved in the [[s:northern-ireland|Ulster]] Cycle of Irish literature, though these tales were written down many centuries later.
voluntii.e: The Voluntii vanish from classical sources after Ptolemy. In early medieval Ireland the [[s:kingdom-of-ulaid|Ulaid]] formed the Kingdom of Ulaid, gradually pushed east of the [[e:river-bann|River Bann]] by the [[e:ui-neill|Uí Néill]].

vingulmark.t: Petty kingdom around the inner Oslofjord, a borderland between Norwegian and Danish power in the early Viking Age.
vingulmark.o: Vingulmark covered lands around the northern Oslofjord, roughly modern Østfold and the area around Oslo. It is known from the sagas as one of the small kingdoms that the kings of [[s:vestfold|Vestfold]] sought to control in the 9th century.
vingulmark.r: The region was close to [[e:denmark|Denmark]] and was often under Danish influence, as was the whole area around the fjord called Viken. Its people farmed the fertile lowlands and traded by sea. No reliable details of its rulers or laws survive.
vingulmark.e: The sagas say [[e:halfdan-the-black|Halfdan the Black]] won Vingulmark and that [[e:harald-fairhair|Harald Fairhair]] held it as part of his realm. Danish kings continued to claim Viken into the 11th century, but the district became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-norway|Kingdom of Norway]].

vakataka-dynasty.t: The leading power of the Deccan in the Gupta age, allied to the Guptas by marriage and patrons of the painted caves of Ajanta.
vakataka-dynasty.o: The dynasty was founded in the mid-3rd century by Vindhyashakti in the area of Vidarbha, as the [[s:satavahana-dynasty|Satavahana dynasty]] broke up. His son Pravarasena I, the only Vakataka to call himself emperor, performed four horse sacrifices and extended rule across central [[e:india|India]] and the northern [[e:deccan|Deccan]]. After him the realm split into a main branch at Nandivardhana and a western branch at Vatsagulma.
vakataka-dynasty.r: The Vakatakas were [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]] who patronised Vedic ritual and Shaiva and Vaishnava cults. Rudrasena II married Prabhavatigupta, daughter of [[e:chandragupta-ii|Chandragupta II]] of the [[s:gupta-empire|Gupta Empire]], who ruled as regent after his death. [[e:pravarasena-ii|Pravarasena II]] wrote the Prakrit poem Setubandha and founded Pravarapura. Under Harishena of the Vatsagulma branch, his minister Varahadeva and other nobles sponsored many of the finest caves at Ajanta.
vakataka-dynasty.e: After Harishena the Vakatakas vanish suddenly in the late 5th century, for reasons that are unclear. Their lands passed to the [[s:vishnukundina-dynasty|Vishnukundina dynasty]], the [[s:kalachuris-of-mahishmati|Kalachuris of Mahishmati]] and the [[s:chalukyas-of-badami|Chalukyas of Badami]].

viscounty-of-carcassonne.t: The Trencavel viscounties of Carcassonne, Béziers and Albi, the heart of Cathar country, destroyed by the Albigensian Crusade in 1209.
viscounty-of-carcassonne.o: In 1067 Raymond Bernard Trencavel, viscount of Albi and Nîmes, gained Carcassonne through his wife Ermengard, heiress of the counts of Carcassonne. Their son [[e:bernard-ato-iv-trencavel|Bernard Ato IV]] built a principality across Carcassonne, Béziers, Albi and Razès, balancing between the counts of [[s:county-of-toulouse|Toulouse]] and Barcelona.
viscounty-of-carcassonne.r: The Trencavels ruled from the walled city of Carcassonne, a centre of Occitan courtly culture. Their lands were the heartland of Catharism, and the viscounts tolerated the dissident church and its followers among the nobility. The Romanesque castle within Carcassonne's walls was their seat.
viscounty-of-carcassonne.e: In 1209 the [[e:albigensian-crusade|Albigensian Crusade]] sacked Béziers and besieged Carcassonne. [[e:raymond-roger-trencavel|Raymond-Roger Trencavel]] surrendered and died in prison, and his lands went to [[e:simon-de-montfort-5th-earl-of-leicester|Simon de Montfort]]. After a failed revolt in 1240 they were absorbed by the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].

venezuela.t: The South American republic that left Gran Colombia in 1830 and, transformed by the world's largest oil reserves, became the Bolivarian Republic under Hugo Chávez.
venezuela.o: In 1830 Venezuela, led by [[e:jose-antonio-paez|José Antonio Páez]], seceded from [[s:gran-colombia|Gran Colombia]] and adopted its own constitution, with Caracas as its capital. Páez dominated the early republic, which abolished [[e:slavery|slavery]] only in 1854.
venezuela.r: The Federal War of 1859 to 1863 gave the country a federal structure, and Antonio Guzmán Blanco modernised Caracas. Under the dictator [[e:juan-vicente-gomez|Juan Vicente Gómez]], from 1908 to 1935, oil was discovered, and Venezuela became a leading exporter. After the fall of Marcos Pérez Jiménez in 1958, the Punto Fijo pact created a two-party democracy. Venezuela co-founded OPEC in 1960 and nationalised its oil industry in 1976.
venezuela.e: [[e:hugo-chavez|Hugo Chávez]], elected in 1998, introduced the 1999 constitution that renamed the state the Bolivarian Republic. Under Nicolás Maduro from 2013, economic collapse drove millions to emigrate. In January 2026 [[s:united-states|United States]] forces captured Maduro in Caracas.

venicones.t: People of Fife and the Tay region recorded by Ptolemy, whose lands later formed a core region of the Picts.
venicones.o: The Venicones appear in [[e:geography-ptolemy|Ptolemy's Geography]] of about 150, generally placed in Fife and perhaps Kinross and southern Angus, between the Forth and the Tay, with a settlement called Orrea. They descended from local [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]] communities living in hillforts, crannogs and open farmsteads on fertile lowland soils.
venicones.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or institutions. Their territory lay close to the Roman frontier: forts along the Gask Ridge and the [[e:legion|legionary]] base at Carpow on the Tay, built under Severus around 208, show heavy Roman activity. Some historians think they are the people later called [[s:maeatae|Maeatae]], or part of them.
venicones.e: The Venicones disappear from the written record after Ptolemy. Their lands later formed the Pictish province of Fib, which gave its name to Fife, within the [[s:kingdom-of-the-picts|Kingdom of the Picts]].

viromandui.t: Belgic people of the upper Somme whose name lives on in the Vermandois and the town of Vermand.
viromandui.o: The Viromandui lived in the upper valleys of the [[e:battle-of-the-somme|Somme]] and Oise, between the [[s:nervii|Nervii]], [[s:ambiani|Ambiani]] and [[s:suessiones|Suessiones]]. Caesar records that they promised ten thousand warriors to the Belgic league of 57 BCE.
viromandui.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions. Excavations at Vermand have revealed a large fortified site of the period.
viromandui.e: They fought beside the [[s:nervii|Nervii]] and [[s:atrebates|Atrebates]] at the Battle of the Sabis in 57 BCE and were defeated. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their chief town became Augusta Viromanduorum (Saint-Quentin), and the medieval [[s:county-of-vermandois|County of Vermandois]] kept their name.

voivodeship-of-serbia-and-banat-of-temes.t: Austrian crown land created after the 1848 revolution in southern Hungary, nominally Serbian but run by imperial officials from Temeschwar.
voivodeship-of-serbia-and-banat-of-temes.o: After the defeat of the Hungarian revolution, Emperor [[e:franz-joseph-i|Franz Joseph]] rewarded the [[e:serbs|Serbs]] who had fought for the dynasty in the [[s:serbian-vojvodina|Serbian Vojvodina]] by creating, in November 1849, a separate crown land from Bačka, Banat and parts of Srem. He took the title of Grand Voivode himself and placed the government at Temeschwar.
voivodeship-of-serbia-and-banat-of-temes.r: The voivodeship was run by German-speaking officials under [[e:vienna|Vienna's]] neo-absolutist system, with a military governor and no elected assembly. Its borders were drawn to include large Romanian, German and Hungarian populations, so [[e:serbs|Serbs]] were only a minority, and Serb leaders were disappointed. Roads, railways and [[e:danube|Danube]] trade developed, and Temeschwar grew as an industrial centre.
voivodeship-of-serbia-and-banat-of-temes.e: As [[e:vienna|Vienna]] sought compromise with [[e:hungary|Hungary]], the crown land was abolished in 1860 and most of its territory returned to the [[s:kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867|Kingdom of Hungary]] (1526-1867), with parts of Srem going to Slavonia. The name survived in the modern Serbian province of Vojvodina.

vanod-state.t: A small estate of the Jhalawad country of northern Kathiawar, on the edge of the Little Rann of Kutch.
vanod-state.o: Vanod was a small holding near the Little [[e:rann-of-kutch|Rann of Kutch]] in the Jhalawad region of Kathiawar, held by a local chiefly family from around 1700. Its founding is known mainly from local tradition.
vanod-state.r: The ruler governed a few dry villages and, after 1807, came under British supervision in the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]]. Little else is recorded.
vanod-state.e: Vanod merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in Surendranagar district.

virumaa.t: North-eastern Estonian county on the Gulf of Finland, conquered by Denmark around 1220 and long a frontier facing Novgorod.
virumaa.o: Virumaa, Vironia in [[e:latin|Latin]], stretched along [[e:estonia|Estonia's]] northern coast towards the Narva river. It was one of the largest ancient Estonian lands, with several parishes and hillforts; its main stronghold, Agelinde, is usually identified with Rakvere.
virumaa.r: Elders led the county's parishes, and its coast gave access to trade with [[s:grand-duchy-of-finland|Finland]] and Novgorod. [[e:henry-of-livonia|Henry of Livonia]] records that Virumaa's elders submitted and accepted baptism under pressure from both the Germans and the Danes, who competed for the land.
virumaa.e: Virumaa passed under Danish rule after 1220, confirmed by the [[e:treaty-of-stensby|Treaty of Stensby]] in 1238, and formed part of the [[s:duchy-of-estonia-1219-1346|Duchy of Estonia]] (1219-1346). Novgorod attacked it repeatedly, notably at the Battle of Wesenberg in 1268. The region later belonged to the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]].

venda-kingdom.t: The kingdom of the Venda in the Soutpansberg mountains, known for its sacred Lake Fundudzi and its resistance to Boer expansion.
venda-kingdom.o: The Singo dynasty moved south across the [[e:limpopo|Limpopo]] from the [[e:zimbabwean-plateau|Zimbabwe plateau]] around 1700, according to tradition, and established its capital at Dzata in the Nzhelele valley. Its rulers brought stone-walling traditions and sacred drums, and they united the Venda of the Soutpansberg under one kingship.
venda-kingdom.r: The king was sacred and secluded, ruling through district chiefs and councillors. Thohoyandou, remembered as the greatest ruler, is said to have vanished mysteriously. Religion centred on ancestors and sacred sites such as Lake Fundudzi, and the domba initiation dance became famous. The Venda traded iron and [[e:copper|copper]] goods, and in 1867 they forced [[e:boers|Boer]] settlers to abandon Schoemansdal.
venda-kingdom.e: After Makhado's death in 1895, the [[s:south-african-republic|South African Republic]] attacked his successor Mphephu in 1898; Mphephu fled across the [[e:limpopo|Limpopo]] and Venda was annexed to the Transvaal. Venda later became a nominally independent apartheid homeland from 1979 to 1994.

vascones.t: The people of Navarre and ancestors of the Basques, whose lands held Pompey's foundation of Pompaelo, modern Pamplona.
vascones.o: The Vascones lived in the upper [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]] valley and western [[e:pyrenees|Pyrenees]], roughly modern [[e:kingdom-of-navarre|Navarre]] and parts of [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]] and La Rioja, by the 3rd century BCE. They probably spoke an early form of Basque, related to Aquitanian across the mountains.
vascones.r: They lived in hill towns and villages, farming the [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]] plain and herding in the mountains. Their towns included Calagurris and later Pompaelo, and they minted coins with Iberian-script legends. They had no single ruler and were organised in local communities.
vascones.e: In the winter of 75 to 74 BCE [[e:pompey|Pompey]] camped in their territory, giving his name to Pompaelo. Calagurris backed Sertorius and fell in 72 BCE after a famous siege. The Vascones were absorbed into [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]], but their language survived and later the [[s:kingdom-of-navarre|Kingdom of Navarre]] arose in their land.

viceroyalty-of-kush.t: Egypt's colonial administration of Nubia in the New Kingdom, governed by the 'King's Son of Kush' and rich in gold.
viceroyalty-of-kush.o: After [[e:thutmose-i|Thutmose I]] destroyed [[s:kerma|Kerma]] around 1500 BCE, the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]] annexed [[e:nubia|Nubia]] as far as the Fourth Cataract. It was governed by a [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]] with the title 'King's Son of Kush', divided into Wawat ([[e:lower-nubia|Lower Nubia]]), administered from Aniba, and Kush ([[e:upper-nubia|Upper Nubia]]).
viceroyalty-of-kush.r: The [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroys]] collected tribute in gold, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], [[e:ebony|ebony]], [[e:cattle|cattle]] and soldiers, and Nubian gold mines in the [[e:wadi-allaqi|Wadi Allaqi]] made [[e:egypt|Egypt]] the richest power of its age. [[e:pharaoh|Pharaohs]] built temple towns at Soleb, Sesebi, Gebel Barkal and Abu Simbel. Nubian elites were educated at the Egyptian court, and Egyptian religion, especially the cult of [[e:amun|Amun]], took deep root. Known viceroys include Merymose and Huy.
viceroyalty-of-kush.e: Around 1080 BCE the [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]] Panehesy fought the [[e:high-priest-of-amun|High Priest of Amun]] in [[s:thebes|Thebes]] and withdrew to [[e:nubia|Nubia]], which then slipped from Egyptian control. Egyptian religion and kingship persisted locally and later inspired the [[e:kushite-empire|Kushite Empire of Napata]].

volcae-tectosages.t: Celtic people of Toulouse, kin of the Galatians of Anatolia, whose sacred gold was seized by a Roman consul in 106 BCE.
volcae-tectosages.o: The Volcae were a Celtic people who settled in Languedoc in the 3rd century BCE. The Tectosages held the western part around Tolosa ([[s:county-of-toulouse|Toulouse]]) on the Garonne. Other bands of the same name joined the migrations into the [[e:balkans|Balkans]] and [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]], where the Galatian Tectosages settled around Ancyra.
volcae-tectosages.r: Tolosa controlled the corridor between the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] and the Atlantic. Strabo describes a rich sanctuary where gold and [[e:silver|silver]] were sunk in sacred lakes. They became allies of [[e:rome|Rome]] after the conquest of the Province in 121 BCE.
volcae-tectosages.e: In 107 BCE they rebelled with the help of the migrating Cimbri and Tigurini. The consul Quintus Servilius Caepio retook Tolosa in 106 BCE and seized its treasure, the gold of Tolosa, which vanished on the way to [[e:rome|Rome]]. Their land became part of [[e:gallia-narbonensis|Gallia Narbonensis]].

vestfold.t: Viking Age kingdom on the west shore of the Oslofjord, home of the Oseberg and Gokstad ship burials and of the dynasty that unified Norway.
vestfold.o: Vestfold's rich farmland and harbours made it a centre of power by the 8th century. The Borre mounds hold one of [[e:scandinavia|Scandinavia's]] largest royal cemeteries, and Frankish annals of 813 record Danish kings campaigning in Vestfold to assert their overlordship, showing it lay in the Danish sphere.
vestfold.r: The kings controlled Kaupang, the trading town the traveller Ohthere called Sciringes heal, where goods from the Frankish, Danish and Arab worlds were exchanged. Royal display reached its height in the Oseberg ship burial of 834 and the Gokstad burial around 900. Snorri's Ynglinga saga traces the kings back to the Swedish Ynglings.
vestfold.e: According to the sagas, [[e:halfdan-the-black|Halfdan the Black]] extended Vestfold's power over the Upplands, and his son [[e:harald-fairhair|Harald Fairhair]] conquered western [[e:norway|Norway]], traditionally at Hafrsfjord around 872. Vestfold thus became the cradle of the [[s:kingdom-of-norway|Kingdom of Norway]], and its ship burials are among the best-known finds of the [[e:viking-age|Viking Age]].

venetian-negroponte.t: Venetian-ruled Euboea, a key Aegean naval base whose fall to Mehmed II in 1470 was one of the great blows to Venice's empire.
venetian-negroponte.o: [[e:venice|Venice]] had long dominated the [[s:triarchy-of-negroponte|Triarchy of Negroponte]] through its bailo in the town of Negroponte ([[s:chalcis|Chalcis]]). As the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] triarchs weakened in the face of the Turks and the Catalans, Venice took over their lands, and by 1390 ruled the whole island directly.
venetian-negroponte.r: A Venetian bailo and councillors governed from the fortified town on the Euripus strait, where a bridge linked the island to the mainland. Negroponte was a major port of call for Venetian [[e:galley|galleys]], a grain and [[e:silk|silk]] market and a base for watching the [[e:aegean|Aegean]]. A Greek [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] majority lived under a [[e:latin|Latin]] elite.
venetian-negroponte.e: In 1470 [[e:mehmed-ii|Mehmed II]] besieged Negroponte by land and sea and stormed it in July; the bailo [[e:paolo-erizzo|Paolo Erizzo]] was killed. The loss shocked [[e:venice|Venice]] and left Euboea Ottoman until the [[e:greek-war-of-independence|Greek War of Independence]].

vyatichi.t: The easternmost East Slavic tribe, settled on the upper Oka, and the last to give up its independence and its pagan gods.
vyatichi.o: The [[e:primary-chronicle|Primary Chronicle]] says the Vyatichi descended from Vyatko, a leader who came from the west, and settled on the upper and middle Oka. Archaeology dates Slavic settlement there to the 8th century, where newcomers mingled with Baltic and Finnic inhabitants. Like their southern neighbours they paid tribute to the [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazars]].
vyatichi.r: Hidden in dense forest far from the [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]], they lived in small fortified settlements under their own chiefs and kept their clan customs. They traded [[e:fur-trade|furs]], honey and wax along the Oka and [[e:volga|Volga]], and hoards of Arab [[e:silver|silver]] [[e:dirham|dirhams]] are common in their lands. They clung to pagan burial rites well into the 12th century, and the missionary Kuksha was killed among them.
vyatichi.e: [[e:sviatoslav-i-of-kiev|Sviatoslav I]] forced them to pay tribute to Kiev in the 960s, Vladimir I subdued them again in 981 and 982, and [[e:vladimir-ii-monomakh|Vladimir Monomakh]] campaigned against their chief Khodota in the late 11th century. Their lands were divided between the principalities of [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]], [[s:grand-principality-of-ryazan|Ryazan]] and Rostov-Suzdal, and later formed the heart of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]].

vyatka-land.t: A remote self-governing land of Russian settlers on the Vyatka river, famous for river pirates and finally conquered by Moscow in 1489.
vyatka-land.o: Settlers from Novgorod and other Russian lands moved into the Vyatka basin among the Udmurt and [[s:mari|Mari]] peoples. A late local tale dates their arrival to 1181, but this is traditional and uncertain. Their main town, Khlynov, later Kirov, is first reliably mentioned in the 14th century.
vyatka-land.r: Vyatka had no princely dynasty for most of its history and was run by assemblies and elected leaders, much like the [[s:novgorod-republic|Novgorod Republic]]. Its people farmed, trapped [[e:fur-trade|furs]] and joined the ushkuiniki, river raiders who attacked towns along the [[e:volga|Volga]] and Kama. It was at times subject to the princes of [[e:nizhny-novgorod|Nizhny Novgorod]] and [[e:moscow|Moscow]] and allied with the Kazan [[e:tatars|Tatars]].
vyatka-land.e: [[e:ivan-iii|Ivan III]] sent a large army against Vyatka in 1489. Khlynov surrendered, its leading men were executed or deported, and the land was annexed to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]]. Its later history is that of an ordinary Russian province.

vediantii.t: Ligurian people of the hills behind Nice whose town Cemenelum became the capital of the Roman Maritime Alps.
vediantii.o: Known from Pliny and Ptolemy, the Vediantii lived in the hills of the lower Var and Paillon valleys, behind the Greek port of Nikaia (Nice), a colony of [[s:massalia|Massalia]].
vediantii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. Like other Alpine [[s:ligures|Ligurians]] they lived in [[e:hill-fort|hill forts]] and practised herding and farming.
vediantii.e: They were brought under Roman control in the Alpine campaigns of Augustus, and in 14 BCE their land became part of the province of Alpes Maritimae. Their settlement of Cemenelum (Cimiez, now part of Nice) became its capital, with an amphitheatre and baths that still survive.

venetian-tinos.t: Venetian-ruled island of Tinos, the last Venetian possession in the Aegean, which held out until 1715 and kept a lasting Catholic community.
venetian-tinos.o: In 1390 the last of the Ghisi family, Giorgio III, died and left the [[s:lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos|Lordship of Tinos and Mykonos]] to [[e:venice|Venice]]. The Republic took over the two islands, first through lessees and later through officials sent from Venice, making Tinos part of its overseas Stato da Mar.
venetian-tinos.r: A Venetian rettore governed from the hilltop fortress of Exobourgo, which protected the islanders from [[e:piracy|pirates]] and Turkish raids. Tinos produced [[e:silk|silk]], wine and other goods, and a significant part of its population became Catholic, alongside an [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] majority. Mykonos was lost to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in 1537, but Tinos repelled several attacks.
venetian-tinos.e: At the start of the Ottoman-Venetian war of 1714-1718, a large Ottoman fleet attacked Tinos in 1715 and its governor surrendered. The Treaty of Passarowitz confirmed Ottoman rule. Tinos still has a substantial Catholic community.

viscounty-of-turenne.t: A self-governing viscounty in the Limousin and Quercy that kept its own estates and tax privileges until it was sold to the French crown in 1738.
viscounty-of-turenne.o: Viscounts of Turenne appear in the late 10th century, based at a castle on a hill near Brive in the [[s:viscounty-of-limoges|Limousin]]. Their lands stretched into Quercy, and the family survived among the competing lords of [[s:duchy-of-aquitaine|Aquitaine]] by playing English and French kings against each other.
viscounty-of-turenne.r: The viscounts enjoyed unusual privileges: the right to summon their own estates, to raise taxes and, by tradition, to mint coin, with near exemption from royal taxation. In 1444 the viscounty passed to the [[e:house-of-la-tour-dauvergne|La Tour d'Auvergne]] family. [[e:henri-de-la-tour-dauvergne-duke-of-bouillon|Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne]], a Huguenot leader, married into the house of [[e:house-of-la-marck|La Marck]] and became prince of [[s:principality-of-sedan|Sedan]].
viscounty-of-turenne.e: In 1738, burdened by debts, Charles-Godefroy de [[e:house-of-la-tour-dauvergne|La Tour d'Auvergne]] sold the viscounty to [[e:louis-xv|Louis XV]], and it was absorbed into the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]]. Its privileges ended, and the region lost its tax exemptions.
ru: Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Duke of Bouillon

vatican-city.t: The world's smallest sovereign state, an enclave in Rome created in 1929 to guarantee the independence of the pope and the Holy See.
vatican-city.o: After [[e:italy|Italy]] took [[e:rome|Rome]] from the [[s:papal-states|Papal States]] in 1870, the popes refused to recognise the loss and considered themselves prisoners in the Vatican. The Roman Question was settled by the [[e:lateran-treaty|Lateran Treaty]] of 11 February 1929, signed by Cardinal Pietro Gasparri for [[e:papacy|Pope]] Pius XI and [[e:benito-mussolini|Benito Mussolini]] for the [[s:kingdom-of-italy|Kingdom of Italy]], creating Vatican City.
vatican-city.r: The state covers about 44 hectares around Saint Peter's Basilica and the Apostolic Palace. The pope is an absolute elective monarch, elected by cardinals in conclave, and governs through a commission and a governor; the Swiss Guard protects him. Vatican City supports the worldwide government of the Holy See, with Vatican Radio founded in 1931, the Vatican Museums and the Apostolic Library.
vatican-city.e: The Second Vatican Council of 1962–1965 transformed the Church's relations with the modern world. The concordat with [[e:italy|Italy]] was revised in 1984. Vatican City continues today; [[e:papacy|Pope]] Leo XIV was elected in 2025.

vacomagi.t: People of north-east Scotland around Moray and Strathspey, to whom Ptolemy assigned four towns, among them Pinnata Castra and Tuesis.
vacomagi.o: [[e:geography-ptolemy|Ptolemy's Geography]] of about 150 places the Vacomagi in the northern Highlands and lowlands, usually located in [[s:kingdom-of-moray|Moray]], Strathspey and parts of Banffshire. He lists four settlements in their land, Bannatia, Tamia, [[e:pinnata-castra|Pinnata Castra]] and Tuesis, more than for most northern peoples, suggesting a well-populated territory.
vacomagi.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. The fertile Laich of [[s:kingdom-of-moray|Moray]] supported farming communities, and the great promontory fort at Burghead, later a major Pictish centre, has sometimes been identified with [[e:pinnata-castra|Pinnata Castra]], though this is uncertain. Roman marching camps reach into the region, showing the passage of Roman armies in the late 1st and early 3rd centuries.
vacomagi.e: The Vacomagi do not appear after Ptolemy. Their lands later formed a heartland of the northern Picts, part of the [[s:kingdom-of-fortriu|Kingdom of Fortriu]] and the wider [[s:kingdom-of-the-picts|Kingdom of the Picts]].

vermont-republic.t: An unrecognised republic in the Green Mountains that governed itself for fourteen years, with the first constitution to ban adult slavery, before joining the United States.
vermont-republic.o: The lands west of the [[e:connecticut-river|Connecticut River]] were claimed by both the [[s:province-of-new-hampshire|Province of New Hampshire]] and the [[s:province-of-new-york|Province of New York]]. Settlers holding [[e:new-hampshire|New Hampshire]] grants resisted [[e:new-york|New York]] through Ethan Allen's Green Mountain Boys, and in 1777 conventions at Westminster and Windsor declared an independent state, first called New Connecticut and then Vermont.
vermont-republic.r: The 1777 constitution prohibited adult [[e:slavery|slavery]], gave the vote to men without property qualifications and set up public schools. [[e:thomas-chittenden|Thomas Chittenden]] served as governor almost throughout. Vermont coined its own money, ran a postal service and naturalised citizens. Congress refused admission while [[e:new-york|New York]] objected, and leaders including the Allens held secret talks with British [[s:province-of-canada|Canada]] in the early 1780s.
vermont-republic.e: Once [[e:new-york|New York]] gave up its claim in 1790 for a payment of $30,000, Vermont was admitted in 1791 as the fourteenth state, the first after the original thirteen. Its constitution became a model for later state charters.

veliocasses.t: Belgic people of the lower Seine whose town Rotomagus became Rouen.
veliocasses.o: The Veliocasses held the Vexin and the lower Seine valley. Caesar reports that they promised warriors to the Belgic league of 57 BCE together with the [[s:viromandui|Viromandui]].
veliocasses.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Their position on the Seine gave them a share of river trade to the Channel.
veliocasses.e: They submitted in 57 BCE and later sent men to relieve Alesia. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their chief town Rotomagus grew into an important river port, the origin of Rouen, later capital of the [[s:duchy-of-normandy|Duchy of Normandy]]. Their name survives in the Vexin.

volaterrae.t: Northern Etruscan city on a lofty hill, master of a large territory and famous for its alabaster urns, which later withstood Sulla for two years.
volaterrae.o: Volaterrae, Etruscan Velathri, modern [[s:commune-of-volterra|Volterra]], occupies a high ridge between the Cecina and Era valleys. Settled from the Villanovan period, it became one of the largest Etruscan cities by the 4th century BCE, when walls more than 7 km long enclosed the town and its fields. Its territory reached the sea and included mines and salt springs.
volaterrae.r: Volaterrae prospered from farming, salt, [[e:copper|copper]] and [[e:timber|timber]]. In the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]] its workshops produced hundreds of carved alabaster and tufa cinerary urns showing mythological scenes and portraits of the dead, now in the Guarnacci Museum. The Porta all'Arco, an arched city gate with sculpted heads, survives. Local families such as the Caecinae remained prominent well into Roman times.
volaterrae.e: Volaterrae became a Roman ally in the 3rd century BCE and supplied grain and [[e:timber|timber]] for Scipio's fleet in 205 BCE. Having backed Marius, it held out against Sulla's siege from 82 to 79 BCE, and later became a municipium. The satirist Persius was born there, and [[s:commune-of-volterra|Volterra]] keeps its alabaster craft.

varahi-state.t: A minor chiefship on the edge of the Rann of Kutch in northern Gujarat.
varahi-state.o: Varahi was a small estate in the dry country of the Banas Kantha region near the [[e:rann-of-kutch|Rann of Kutch]], held by a local chiefly family from around 1700. Its founding is poorly documented.
varahi-state.r: The ruler held a few villages of grazing and [[e:millet|millet]] land. In the British period Varahi was a minor state under the [[e:banas-kantha-agency|Banas Kantha Agency]]. Little else is recorded.
varahi-state.e: Varahi merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in Patan district.

viducasses.t: Small Gallic people of the Caen plain whose Roman town at Vieux has yielded the famous Thorigny marble.
viducasses.o: Known from Pliny and Ptolemy, the Viducasses lived south of modern Caen in lower [[s:duchy-of-normandy|Normandy]]. They were probably included among the Armorican peoples in Caesar's time.
viducasses.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. Their chief town, Aregenua, lay at Vieux.
viducasses.e: Under [[e:rome|Rome]] Aregenua became a prosperous civitas capital with baths and fine houses. The Thorigny marble, an inscription of 238 CE, honours one of its citizens, Titus Sennius Sollemnis. The civitas later merged with that of the [[s:baiocasses|Baiocasses]].

viceroyalty-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.t: The last viceroyalty created by Spain in the Americas, ruled from Buenos Aires, whose crisis in 1810 began Argentina's independence.
viceroyalty-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.o: To counter Portuguese expansion and smuggling, [[e:charles-iii-of-spain|Charles III]] created the Viceroyalty of the [[e:rio-de-la-plata|Río de la Plata]] in 1776, with [[e:buenos-aires|Buenos Aires]] as its capital and [[e:pedro-de-cevallos|Pedro de Cevallos]] as first [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]]. It joined the [[e:governorate|governorates]] of Buenos Aires, [[s:republic-of-paraguay|Paraguay]] and Tucumán with Cuyo and the [[s:royal-audiencia-of-charcas|Royal Audiencia of Charcas]], including the [[e:silver|silver]] of [[e:potosi|Potosí]].
viceroyalty-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.r: [[e:silver|Silver]] from [[e:potosi|Potosí]] now flowed out through [[e:buenos-aires|Buenos Aires]], which boomed after the free-trade regulation of 1778 opened it to direct trade with [[e:spain|Spain]]. Intendancies replaced the old [[e:governorate|governorates]] in 1782. Hides and salted meat were growing exports. In 1806 and 1807 British forces invaded Buenos Aires and Montevideo, and local militias under [[e:santiago-de-liniers|Santiago de Liniers]] drove them out, boosting [[e:criollo-people|Creole]] confidence.
viceroyalty-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.e: After [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] capture of the Spanish king, the May Revolution of 1810 deposed the [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]] and created the [[s:united-provinces-of-the-rio-de-la-plata|United Provinces of the Río de la Plata]]. [[s:republic-of-paraguay|Paraguay]] and [[s:royal-audiencia-of-charcas|Upper Peru]] broke away, and royalist Montevideo fell in 1814.

vajji.t: A confederation of republican clans around Vaishali, praised by the Buddha for its assemblies and remembered as one of the world's early republics.
vajji.o: The Vajji league formed north of the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges]] in modern Bihar, uniting eight or nine clans. The most powerful were the [[e:licchavi|Licchavis]] of [[e:vaishali|Vaishali]]; others included the Videhas of Mithila and the Jnatrikas, the clan of Mahavira, the Jain teacher, who was born near Vaishali. By the 6th century BCE it was one of the sixteen mahajanapadas.
vajji.r: The Vajjis were governed by assemblies of the heads of noble families, who met in council and elected leaders. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta the Buddha says the Vajjis will prosper as long as they meet often, act in concord and honour their traditions. [[e:vaishali|Vaishali]] was a large trading city with many shrines and was visited often by both the Buddha and Mahavira.
vajji.e: Ajatashatru of the [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Kingdom of Magadha]] built a fort at Pataligrama, the future [[e:pataliputra|Pataliputra]], and sent his minister Vassakara to sow discord among the Vajjis before conquering them after a long war in the 5th century BCE. [[e:vaishali|Vaishali]] later hosted the Second Buddhist Council.

visby.t: Walled Hanseatic town on Gotland, one of the great trading centres of the medieval Baltic, whose walls and churches still stand.
visby.o: Visby grew on Gotland's west coast as a harbour of the [[s:gotland|Gotland]] farmers' republic. In 1161 [[e:henry-the-lion|Henry the Lion]] of Saxony confirmed the rights of German merchants trading on Gotland, and German traders settled alongside Gotlanders, making Visby the base of the Community of Gotland Merchants who traded with Novgorod.
visby.r: The town was run by a council of German and Gotlandic merchants and acted with growing independence from the rural island. Around 1300 it built a 3.4-kilometre stone wall, and it filled with stone warehouses and more than a dozen churches. Its maritime law influenced other Baltic ports, and it was a leading member of the early [[s:hanseatic-league|Hanseatic League]].
visby.e: Conflict with the rural Gotlanders led to civil war in 1288. In 1361 [[e:valdemar-iv-of-denmark|Valdemar IV of Denmark]] took Visby after defeating the farmers outside its walls, and the town surrendered. Its importance declined as [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck|Lübeck]] rose. Visby is now a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|World Heritage Site]].

viscounty-of-limoges.t: A viscounty in the Limousin that outlasted most feudal lordships and passed by inheritance to Brittany, Albret and finally the future Henry IV.
viscounty-of-limoges.o: Viscounts appear at Limoges in the late 9th century as deputies of the counts of [[s:county-of-poitou|Poitou]], who as dukes of [[s:duchy-of-aquitaine|Aquitaine]] claimed overlordship of the Limousin. The office became hereditary in a local family, which governed the city's castle quarter while the [[e:bishop|bishop]] and the abbey of Saint-Martial dominated the rest of the town.
viscounty-of-limoges.r: The viscounts were middling lords caught between [[s:duchy-of-aquitaine|Aquitaine]], the Plantagenet kings and the French crown, often clashing with their own townsmen and with English overlords; Richard the Lionheart died in 1199 besieging Châlus, a castle in the viscounty. Limoges itself was known for its enamel work and as a pilgrimage centre on the road to Compostela.
viscounty-of-limoges.e: Through marriage the viscounty passed to the dukes of [[s:duchy-of-brittany|Brittany]] in 1275, then to the Blois-Penthièvre line and the house of Albret. It reached the [[e:house-of-bourbon|Bourbons]] through [[e:jeanne-dalbret|Jeanne d'Albret]], and when her son [[e:henry-iv-of-france|Henry IV]] became king in 1589 it was merged with the crown.

varsoda-state.t: A minor Rajput chiefship on the Sabarmati in northern Gujarat, one of the small estates of the Mahi Kantha country.
varsoda-state.o: Varsoda was one of the petty estates of the [[e:mahi-kantha-agency|Mahi Kantha]] region, held by a [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] family from around 1600. Its early history is known mainly from local tradition.
varsoda-state.r: The Thakor ruled a few villages, paid tribute through the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads of Baroda]] and was supervised by the [[e:mahi-kantha-agency|British Mahi Kantha Agency]]. Few details of its rulers are recorded in standard works.
varsoda-state.e: Varsoda was merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in present Gandhinagar district.

vettones.t: A Celtic-speaking people of the western Meseta, known for their great hillforts and the stone boars and bulls called verracos.
vettones.o: The Vettones emerged in the second half of the first millennium BCE between the Douro and [[e:tagus|Tagus]] rivers, in modern Ávila, Salamanca and Cáceres and parts of Portugal. They grew out of the [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]] Cogotas culture and were related to their Lusitanian and Celtiberian neighbours.
vettones.r: They lived in large fortified hillforts such as Las Cogotas, Ulaca and El Raso, and their economy was dominated by [[e:cattle|cattle]] and pig herding. Hundreds of granite sculptures of boars and bulls, the verracos, mark their territory and probably protected herds or pastures. Their society had warrior elites, and they spoke a Celtic or para-Celtic language.
vettones.e: Often allied with the [[s:lusitanians|Lusitanians]], they resisted [[e:rome|Rome]] through the 2nd century BCE and were finally subdued after campaigns including [[e:julius-caesar|Julius Caesar's]] of 61 BCE. Their lands became part of the province of [[s:lusitania|Lusitania]], with towns such as Salmantica and Augustobriga.

voivodeship-of-seneslau.t: Romanian voivodeship east of the Olt, one of the earliest Romanian polities recorded, known from a Hungarian royal charter of 1247.
voivodeship-of-seneslau.o: The only clear source is the charter of 1247 by which [[e:bela-iv-of-hungary|Béla IV of Hungary]] granted lands to the [[e:knights-hospitaller|Knights Hospitaller]]. It mentions the land of Seneslau, voivode of the [[e:romanians|Romanians]] (Olati), east of the Olt in what became [[s:principality-of-wallachia|Wallachia]], which was left in Romanian hands.
voivodeship-of-seneslau.r: Nothing is known of its government beyond the charter, which treats Seneslau as a tributary of the Hungarian crown, obliged to share revenues and provide military aid. His power probably rested on local knezes and the routes between the Carpathians and the [[e:danube|Danube]].
voivodeship-of-seneslau.e: It is not mentioned again, and its fate is unknown. Historians see it as one of the polities later united in the [[s:principality-of-wallachia|Principality of Wallachia]] by Basarab I.

vladimir-suzdal.t: The grand principality of north-eastern Rus', centre of white-stone architecture and the political root of Muscovite Russia.
vladimir-suzdal.o: In 1157 [[e:andrei-bogolyubsky|Andrei Bogolyubsky]], son of [[e:yuri-dolgoruky|Yuri Dolgoruky]], moved the capital of the [[s:principality-of-rostov-suzdal|Principality of Rostov-Suzdal]] to Vladimir on the Klyazma. He built the [[e:golden-gate-vladimir|Golden Gate]], the Dormition Cathedral and the Church of the Intercession on the Nerl, and in 1169 his army sacked Kiev, though he stayed in the north.
vladimir-suzdal.r: Andrei was murdered by his boyars in 1174, and his brother [[e:vsevolod-the-big-nest|Vsevolod the Big Nest]] ruled from 1176 to 1212, dominating north-eastern Rus' and fathering many princes. After the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] sacked Vladimir in 1238 and killed Yuri II on the Sit river, the grand-princely title was granted by the khans of the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]] through a patent, the yarlyk, while the land split into [[e:appanage|appanages]].
vladimir-suzdal.e: [[e:alexander-nevsky|Alexander Nevsky]] held the title from 1252, and his descendants in [[e:moscow|Moscow]] and the princes of Tver fought for it. In 1331 Ivan I Kalita of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]] became sole grand prince, and Vladimir's title was merged into Moscow's.
