vandal-kingdom.t: The Germanic kingdom of the Vandals and Alans in North Africa, whose fleet sacked Rome in 455 and dominated the western Mediterranean.
vandal-kingdom.o: The [[e:vandals|Vandals]] and [[s:alans|Alans]] crossed the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] in 406 and entered [[e:spain|Spain]] in 409. In 429 King Gaiseric led them across the [[e:strait-of-gibraltar|Strait of Gibraltar]] into [[e:africa|Africa]]. A treaty of 435 made them federates of the [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]], but in 439 Gaiseric seized [[e:carthage|Carthage]], taking [[s:africa-proconsularis|Africa Proconsularis]], the richest western province.
vandal-kingdom.r: Gaiseric ruled as an independent king, confiscating Roman estates for his followers while keeping Roman administration and [[e:latin|Latin]] culture. The [[e:vandals|Vandals]] were [[e:arianism|Arian Christians]] and at times persecuted Nicene clergy, most harshly under Huneric. Their fleet took [[e:sicily|Sicily]], [[e:sardinia|Sardinia]], [[s:corsican-republic|Corsica]] and the Balearics, and in 455 sacked [[e:rome|Rome]]. [[e:berber-revolt|Berber revolts]], such as that of the [[s:kingdom-of-the-aures|Kingdom of the Aures]], cut away the interior.
vandal-kingdom.e: In 530 Gelimer deposed the pro-Roman king Hilderic, giving Justinian a pretext to invade. Belisarius won at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum in 533, and Gelimer surrendered in 534. [[e:africa|Africa]] became the [[s:praetorian-prefecture-of-africa|Praetorian Prefecture of Africa]], and the [[e:vandals|Vandals]] vanished as a people.

vishalgad-state.t: A Maratha jagir under Kolhapur held by a branch of the Pant Pratinidhi family, named after the hill fort of Vishalgad.
vishalgad-state.o: Vishalgad took its name from the Sahyadri fort where [[e:shivaji|Shivaji]] took refuge in 1660. Around 1700 the fort and its lands were held by a branch of the family of the [[e:pant-pratinidhi|Pant Pratinidhi]], ministers of the [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] kings, as feudatories of [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur]].
vishalgad-state.r: The chiefs governed a hilly territory in the [[e:western-ghats|Western Ghats]] from Malkapur, under the overlordship of [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur]] and British supervision through the Kolhapur residency. Few further details of its rulers are widely recorded.
vishalgad-state.e: Vishalgad merged with [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur]] into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1949 and became part of Maharashtra in 1960. Its lands lie in Kolhapur district.

votadini.t: People of south-east Scotland and Northumberland centred on Traprain Law, who lived beside Roman Britain and became the post-Roman Gododdin.
votadini.o: Ptolemy places the Votadini on the east coast between the [[e:firth-of-forth|Firth of Forth]] and the Tyne in the 2nd century. They descended from [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]] communities of Lothian and the Borders, and their great hillfort at [[e:traprain-law|Traprain Law]] in East Lothian was a major centre from before the Roman arrival in the 80s.
votadini.r: Unlike neighbours such as the [[s:selgovae|Selgovae]], the Votadini show few signs of hostility to [[e:rome|Rome]], and many historians think they were a friendly buffer people beyond [[e:hadrians-wall|Hadrian's Wall]]. Roman goods reached [[e:traprain-law|Traprain Law]] in quantity, culminating in the Traprain Law Treasure, a hoard of cut Roman [[e:silver|silver]] buried in the early 5th century, perhaps a payment or subsidy. Their economy rested on mixed farming.
votadini.e: After Roman rule ended, the Votadini developed into the [[s:kingdom-of-gododdin|Kingdom of Gododdin]], centred on [[e:din-eidyn|Din Eidyn]], Edinburgh, whose warriors are celebrated in the Welsh poem Y Gododdin. Their name in its Welsh form, Guotodin, carried the people into the early [[e:middle-ages|medieval period]].

volga-bulgaria.t: A Muslim Bulgar state on the middle Volga that grew rich on the fur trade and was the northernmost outpost of Islam for three centuries.
volga-bulgaria.o: [[e:bulgars|Bulgar]] tribes who left [[s:old-great-bulgaria|Old Great Bulgaria]] after the [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazar]] conquest moved north to the confluence of the [[e:volga|Volga]] and Kama during the 7th and 8th centuries, ruling over Finnic and other local peoples. They remained tributaries of the Khazars until the 10th century, when the Khazar state weakened.
volga-bulgaria.r: In 922 the ruler Almish received an embassy from the Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliph]], described by [[e:ahmad-ibn-fadlan|Ibn Fadlan]], and adopted [[e:islam|Islam]]. Bolghar and later Bilyar were large trading cities where [[e:fur-trade|furs]], honey, wax and slaves from the north were exchanged for Islamic [[e:silver|silver]] and goods. The [[e:emir|emirs]] minted coins and fought frequent wars with [[s:kievan-rus|Kievan Rus']] and [[s:vladimir-suzdal|Vladimir-Suzdal]].
volga-bulgaria.e: The [[e:bulgars|Bulgars]] defeated a Mongol force at the Samara Bend in 1223, but in 1236 the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] returned, destroyed Bilyar and conquered the country. It became part of the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]], with Bolghar briefly serving as a Horde capital. Both the [[e:volga|Volga]] [[e:tatars|Tatars]] and the Chuvash claim the Bulgars among their ancestors.

venetian-ionian-islands.t: Venice's possessions in the Ionian Sea, centred on Corfu, which stayed outside Ottoman rule and took on a lasting Italian character.
venetian-ionian-islands.o: In 1386 [[s:corcyra|Corfu]], previously under the Angevins of Naples, placed itself under Venetian protection; [[e:venice|Venice]] formally bought the rights in 1402. It later added Zakynthos (1485), Cephalonia and Ithaca (1500) and finally [[s:leucas|Lefkada]] (1684), while Kythira was already Venetian, gaining control over the sea route between the Adriatic and the eastern [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]].
venetian-ionian-islands.r: A Venetian provveditore generale in [[s:corcyra|Corfu]] governed with local councils of island nobles registered in a Golden Book. Italian became the language of administration and the elite, while the majority stayed Greek [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]]. [[e:olive-oil|Olive oil]] and currants were the main exports. Corfu's fortresses withstood Ottoman sieges in 1537 and 1716, the latter under Johann Matthias von der Schulenburg.
venetian-ionian-islands.e: When [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] ended the Venetian Republic in 1797, the [[e:treaty-of-campo-formio|Treaty of Campo Formio]] gave the islands to [[e:france|France]], creating the [[s:french-ionian-islands|French Ionian Islands]]. Their distinct Italian-Greek culture survived into the [[s:septinsular-republic|Septinsular Republic]] and British rule.

visigothic-kingdom.t: Gothic kingdom first at Toulouse, then at Toledo, that ruled Iberia for two centuries until the Muslim conquest of 711.
visigothic-kingdom.o: After sacking [[e:rome|Rome]] in 410 under Alaric, the [[e:visigoths|Visigoths]] moved into Gaul and [[e:spain|Spain]]. In 418 Rome settled them as federates in [[s:duchy-of-aquitaine|Aquitaine]], with [[s:county-of-toulouse|Toulouse]] as their capital, under King Wallia. Theodoric I died fighting Attila on the [[e:battle-of-the-catalaunian-plains|Catalaunian Plains]] in 451, and Euric made the kingdom fully independent and expanded deep into Hispania.
visigothic-kingdom.r: Gothic warriors ruled a mostly Roman population, at first under separate laws. The kings were Arian until Reccared converted to [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] in 589, after which the Councils of [[e:toledo|Toledo]] became central to government. Leovigild conquered the [[s:kingdom-of-the-suebi|Kingdom of the Suebi]], and Recceswinth issued the Visigothic Code in 654.
visigothic-kingdom.e: [[e:clovis-i|Clovis]] defeated [[e:alaric-ii|Alaric II]] at Vouillé in 507, and the centre of the kingdom shifted to Hispania, where [[e:toledo|Toledo]] became the capital by the 560s. In 711 [[e:tariq-ibn-ziyad|Tariq ibn Ziyad]] defeated King Roderic, and the [[s:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]] conquered [[e:iberia|Iberia]]; the last Visigothic outpost in Septimania fell around 720. The Christian kingdoms of the north claimed Visigothic descent.

vichy-france.t: The authoritarian French State of Marshal Pétain, which collaborated with Nazi Germany and helped deport Jews from France.
vichy-france.o: After the German victory in 1940 and the [[e:armistice-of-11-november-1918|armistice]] of 22 June, [[e:france|France]] was divided into an occupied north and an unoccupied south. On 10 July the parliament meeting at Vichy voted full powers to Marshal Philippe Pétain, ending the [[s:french-third-republic|French Third Republic]] and creating the French State.
vichy-france.r: Pétain led a 'National Revolution' under the motto Work, Family, Fatherland, abolishing parliament and promoting conservative Catholic values. Vichy chose collaboration after Pétain met Hitler at Montoire in 1940. Its own anti-Jewish laws and its police's role in round-ups, such as the Vel d'Hiv in 1942, contributed to the [[e:deportation|deportation]] of about 76,000 [[e:jews|Jews]] from [[e:france|France]].
vichy-france.e: [[e:germany|Germany]] occupied the south in November 1942, leaving Vichy little power. After the Allied landings of 1944 the regime collapsed; its leaders were taken to Sigmaringen in Germany. Pétain was sentenced to death, commuted to life imprisonment, and [[e:pierre-laval|Pierre Laval]] was executed.

velabri.t: People of south-west Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, usually placed on the Atlantic coast of Kerry beside the Iverni.
velabri.o: The Velabri are known only from [[e:geography-ptolemy|Ptolemy's Geography]] of about 150, which places them on the south-west coast of Ireland, south of the [[s:gangani-ireland|Gangani (Ireland)]] and west of the [[s:iverni|Iverni]], roughly in modern County [[s:ciarraige-luachra|Kerry]]. Ptolemy's information on Ireland came from earlier reports by sailors along the Atlantic coast.
velabri.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or customs. The peninsulas of [[s:ciarraige-luachra|Kerry]] were a land of stone forts, promontory forts and pastoral farming, and the region later produced many ogham stones, showing that Irish-speaking communities with strong lineage traditions lived there by the 5th century.
velabri.e: The Velabri do not appear in any later source, and no Irish population name has been securely matched with theirs. Their region later formed part of the [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Kingdom of Munster]] and the lands of peoples such as the [[e:corcu-duibne|Corcu Duibne]] and the [[s:ciarraige-luachra|Ciarraige Luachra]].

vestini.t: Sabellic people of the Gran Sasso and the Aterno valley in Abruzzo, whose territory produced the famous Warrior of Capestrano statue.
vestini.o: The Vestini lived in the high valleys around the [[e:gran-sasso|Gran Sasso]] and the middle Aterno, reaching the Adriatic coast near Pinna (Penne). Ancient writers counted them among the Sabellian peoples; their culture developed locally from the early 1st millennium BCE.
vestini.r: They lived in scattered villages, [[e:hill-fort|hill forts]] and towns such as Pinna, Aveia and Peltuinum, keeping flocks that moved between mountain and lowland pastures. The Warrior of Capestrano, a life-size limestone statue of the 6th century BCE with a South Picene inscription, was found in a Vestine cemetery and is the most famous work of Italic sculpture. Their political organisation is otherwise poorly known.
vestini.e: Allied with the [[s:samnite-league|Samnites]], the Vestini were defeated by [[e:rome|Rome]] in 325 BCE and made an alliance around 302 BCE. They joined the Italian revolt in the [[e:social-war-91-87-bce|Social War]] and were defeated in 89 BCE, then received citizenship and were absorbed into Roman [[e:italy|Italy]].

voivodeship-of-transylvania.t: Eastern province of medieval Hungary ruled by royal voivodes, home to Hungarian nobles, Saxons and Székelys, which became an autonomous principality in 1570.
voivodeship-of-transylvania.o: After Stephen I annexed the [[s:realm-of-the-gyulas|Realm of the Gyulas]] in 1003, [[s:principality-of-transylvania|Transylvania]] was organised in royal counties. From 1176, when Leustach is named voivode, a royal official with that Slavic title governed the province for the kings of [[e:hungary|Hungary]].
voivodeship-of-transylvania.r: The voivode headed the counties of the nobility, while German settlers ([[s:saxons|Saxons]]) had their own rights under the Andreanum of 1224 and the Székelys formed a separate military community. [[e:romanians|Romanians]] formed much of the peasantry. Voivodes such as [[e:ladislaus-kan|Ladislaus Kán]] around 1300 acted almost as independent rulers. After a peasant revolt in 1437, nobles, [[e:saxons|Saxons]] and Székelys formed the Union of Three Nations, which excluded Romanians. [[e:john-hunyadi|John Hunyadi]] served as voivode from 1441.
voivodeship-of-transylvania.e: After Mohács in 1526, voivode [[e:john-zapolya|John Zápolya]] became king of eastern [[e:hungary|Hungary]]. His son [[e:john-sigismund-zapolya|John Sigismund]] renounced the royal title by the Treaty of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-speyer|Speyer]] in 1570, and the land became the [[s:principality-of-transylvania|Principality of Transylvania]] under Ottoman overlordship.

viceroyalty-of-new-granada.t: The Spanish viceroyalty of northern South America, ruled from Bogotá, whose collapse in the wars of independence gave rise to Gran Colombia.
viceroyalty-of-new-granada.o: [[e:spain|Spain]] created the Viceroyalty of [[e:new-granada|New Granada]] in 1717 out of the [[s:new-kingdom-of-granada|New Kingdom of Granada]] and other territories of the [[s:viceroyalty-of-peru|Viceroyalty of Peru]], to defend the [[e:caribbean|Caribbean]] coast and improve administration. Abolished in 1723 for lack of revenue, it was permanently restored in 1739, covering modern [[s:republic-of-colombia|Colombia]], [[s:republic-of-ecuador|Ecuador]], [[s:republic-of-panama|Panama]] and [[s:venezuela|Venezuela]].
viceroyalty-of-new-granada.r: The [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]] ruled from [[e:bogota|Santa Fe de Bogotá]]. [[e:carthago-nova|Cartagena's]] fortifications withstood the British attack under [[e:edward-vernon|Edward Vernon]] in 1741, led by Blas de Lezo and Viceroy Sebastián de Eslava. Gold from the Chocó and Antioquia was the main export. In 1777 [[s:venezuela|Venezuela]] was separated as a captaincy general. The Comunero revolt of 1781 opposed new taxes. The Royal Botanical Expedition of José Celestino Mutis from 1783 trained a generation of [[e:criollo-people|Creole]] scientists.
viceroyalty-of-new-granada.e: A junta in [[e:bogota|Bogotá]] on 20 July 1810 began the movement for independence. [[e:pablo-morillo|Pablo Morillo]] reconquered the territory in 1816, but [[e:simon-bolivar|Simón Bolívar's]] victory at Boyacá in 1819 ended Spanish rule and led to the creation of [[s:gran-colombia|Gran Colombia]].

vistulans.t: A West Slavic tribe of the upper Vistula, centred on Krakow, whose pagan prince was warned by Saint Methodius to accept baptism.
vistulans.o: The Vistulans settled the upper Vistula basin in what is now southern [[e:poland|Poland]], with their centre on Wawel Hill in Krakow and another stronghold at Wislica. They are named in the 9th-century list known as the Bavarian Geographer and in the Life of Saint Methodius.
vistulans.r: Their territory was a fertile, densely settled region on trade routes between [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]], [[s:great-moravia|Moravia]] and Rus', and the rich hill fort at Wawel suggests a wealthy ruling elite. The Life of Methodius tells of a powerful pagan prince on the Vistula who persecuted Christians and was urged to be baptised willingly before he was baptised by force in a foreign land.
vistulans.e: The prophecy seems to have come true when Svatopluk of [[s:great-moravia|Great Moravia]] brought the Vistulans under his rule around 880. After [[e:moravia|Moravia]] collapsed, the region passed to the [[s:duchy-of-bohemia|Duchy of Bohemia]], and around 990 the [[s:duchy-of-poland|Duchy of Poland]] took Krakow, which later became the Polish royal capital.

viceroyalty-of-peru.t: Spain's great South American viceroyalty, ruled from Lima, whose silver from Potosí flowed across the world for nearly three centuries.
viceroyalty-of-peru.o: [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]] created the Viceroyalty of Peru through the [[e:new-laws|New Laws of 1542]], replacing the [[e:governorate|governorates]] of [[e:governorate-of-new-castile|New Castile]] and [[e:governorate-of-new-toledo|New Toledo]]. The first [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]], Blasco Núñez Vela, was killed by rebels under [[e:gonzalo-pizarro|Gonzalo Pizarro]] in 1546, and royal authority was only restored when Pedro de la Gasca defeated Pizarro in 1548.
viceroyalty-of-peru.r: [[e:viceroy-of-india|Viceroy]] [[e:francisco-alvarez-de-toledo|Francisco de Toledo]], from 1569 to 1581, reorganised the colony: indigenous people were moved into reducciones, and the [[e:mita|mita]] drafted labour for the [[e:silver|silver]] mines of [[e:potosi|Potosí]] and the mercury mines of Huancavelica. Lima, the City of the Kings, was home to the [[e:audiencia|Audiencia]], the University of San Marcos, founded in 1551, and the [[e:portuguese-inquisition|Inquisition]]. Its territory at first covered nearly all of Spanish [[e:south-america|South America]].
viceroyalty-of-peru.e: The [[e:bourbon-reforms|Bourbon reforms]] removed [[e:new-granada|New Granada]] in 1717 and [[e:rio-de-la-plata|Río de la Plata]] in 1776. After the revolt of [[e:tupac-amaru|Túpac Amaru]] II in 1780 was crushed, [[e:peru|Peru]] remained a royalist stronghold until [[e:jose-de-san-martin|San Martín]] proclaimed independence in 1821 and the Battle of Ayacucho in 1824 ended Spanish rule.

vanni-chieftaincies.t: A belt of semi-independent chiefdoms in the dry forests of northern Sri Lanka, held by Vanniyar chiefs for over five centuries.
vanni-chieftaincies.o: After the collapse of the Polonnaruwa kingdom in the 13th century, the dry zone between the Jaffna peninsula and the Sinhalese heartland was left largely to local military chiefs known as Vanniyars. Their chiefdoms, often called the Vanni, emerged gradually and are poorly documented in the early period.
vanni-chieftaincies.r: The Vanni chiefs ruled scattered villages of [[e:rice|rice]] farmers and forest dwellers, paying tribute in elephants, honey and grain to whichever overlord was strongest: the [[s:jaffna-kingdom|Jaffna Kingdom]], the [[s:kingdom-of-kotte|Kingdom of Kotte]] or later the [[s:kingdom-of-kandy|Kingdom of Kandy]]. Both Tamil and Sinhalese chiefs existed, and the region kept its own customs and loyalties.
vanni-chieftaincies.e: The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and then the British sought to subdue the Vanni. The last important chief, [[e:pandara-vanniyan|Pandara Vanniyan]], resisted the British and was defeated in 1803, after which the area was absorbed into [[s:british-ceylon|British Ceylon]]. He is remembered as a hero of Tamil resistance.

virpur-state.t: A small Jadeja Rajput state in central Kathiawar whose town is now a major pilgrimage centre of the saint Jalaram.
virpur-state.o: Virpur, also called Virpur-Kherdi, was held by a branch of [[e:jadeja|Jadeja Rajputs]] related to the ruling houses of Nawanagar and [[s:gondal-state|Gondal]]. It emerged as a separate holding around 1600.
virpur-state.r: The Thakor ruled a small agrarian territory, paying tribute to the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads of Baroda]] and [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh]] before British supervision in the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]] after 1807. In the 19th century the town became the home of the saint Jalaram, whose free kitchen drew devotees from across [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].
virpur-state.e: Virpur merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960. The Jalaram temple in [[s:rajkot-state|Rajkot]] district keeps the town well known.

veneti.t: Seafaring Gallic people of southern Brittany who controlled Atlantic trade with Britain until Caesar destroyed their fleet in 56 BCE.
veneti.o: The [[s:ancient-veneti|Veneti]] held the coast of the Morbihan, a landscape of tidal inlets and promontories, with Darioritum (Vannes) as their later chief town. They dominated the sea routes between Armorica and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and were the strongest of the Armorican peoples.
veneti.r: Caesar describes their tall oak ships with flat bottoms, iron bolts and leather sails, built to ride Atlantic storms, and their towns set on headlands cut off by the tide. They levied tolls on other seafarers and grew rich on trade in [[e:tin|tin]] and goods with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]].
veneti.e: In 56 BCE they detained Roman officers sent for grain, and Caesar built a fleet on the Loire. Decimus Brutus defeated them in a calm, probably in [[e:battle-of-quiberon-bay|Quiberon Bay]], by cutting their rigging with hooked poles. Caesar executed their council and sold the people into [[e:slavery|slavery]]; Vannes keeps their name.

vetulonia.t: Early Etruscan power in the metal-rich hills of northern Etruria, which Roman tradition credited as the source of the fasces and other symbols of office.
vetulonia.o: Vetulonia, Etruscan Vatluna, grew on a hill overlooking the former [[e:lake-prile|Lake Prile]], then a lagoon open to the sea, in the 9th and 8th centuries BCE. Its wealth came from the [[e:copper|copper]], iron and [[e:silver|silver]] of the nearby Colline Metallifere, and it was one of the leading Etruscan centres of the 8th and 7th centuries BCE.
vetulonia.r: Rich 'circle tombs' and great tumuli such as the Pietrera reveal an aristocracy enriched by metals and trade with [[e:sardinia|Sardinia]] and the eastern [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]]. Its goldsmiths excelled in granulation. The 'Tomb of the Lictor' contained an iron double axe with rods, and the Roman poet Silius Italicus wrote that [[e:rome|Rome]] borrowed the fasces, curule chair and purple-bordered toga from Vetulonia.
vetulonia.e: Vetulonia declined from the 6th century BCE as [[s:populonia|Populonia]] and [[s:rusellae|Rusellae]] grew. It revived in the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]], minting coins, and passed under Roman control in the early 3rd century BCE, later becoming a municipium. Its exact location was only confirmed in the 19th century; the village of Colonna di Buriano took the ancient name in 1887.

viceroyalty-of-carchemish.t: The Hittite viceroyalty of Carchemish, which governed Syria for the Hittite kings and outlived the empire's fall.
viceroyalty-of-carchemish.o: [[e:suppiluliuma-i|Suppiluliuma I]] of the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]] took [[s:kingdom-of-carchemish|Carchemish]], a great [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] crossing city, after a siege c. 1327 BCE, ending the [[e:mitanni|Mitanni Empire's]] hold on [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]]. He made his son Piyassili, known by the Hurrian name Sharri-Kushuh, king of Carchemish.
viceroyalty-of-carchemish.r: The kings of [[s:kingdom-of-carchemish|Carchemish]] acted as [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroys]] for the Hittite great king, supervising Syrian [[e:vassal|vassals]] such as [[s:kingdom-of-ugarit|Ugarit]], [[s:emar|Emar]] and [[s:kingdom-of-amurru|Amurru]], settling their disputes and collecting tribute. They belonged to the Hittite royal family and kept a court with Hurrian and Luwian traditions.
viceroyalty-of-carchemish.e: When [[e:hattusa|Hattusa]] fell around 1180 BCE, [[s:kingdom-of-carchemish|Carchemish]] survived. Kuzi-Teshub took the title great king, and his heirs founded the Neo-Hittite Kingdom of Carchemish and kingdoms such as [[s:melid|Melid]], carrying Hittite traditions into the [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]].

velanati-chodas.t: A Telugu Choda family of the Krishna delta that rose as Chola vassals and briefly dominated coastal Andhra in the 12th century.
velanati-chodas.o: The Velanati Chodas were a family of chiefs from Velanadu, the region around Guntur in coastal Andhra. In the late 11th century they rose as feudatories of the [[e:chola-empire|Chola]] emperor Kulottunga I, who had absorbed the lands of the [[s:eastern-chalukyas|Eastern Chalukyas]], and governed the Vengi region on his behalf from Chandavolu, near Tenali.
velanati-chodas.r: As [[e:chola-empire|Chola]] power in Andhra weakened in the 12th century, [[e:gonka-ii|Gonka II]] and his successors ruled much of the coastal region between the Krishna and the Godavari independently, though still using Chola titles. They patronised Shaiva and Vaishnava temples and Telugu inscriptions record their grants. The kingdom was drawn into the wars of local chiefs, including the conflict remembered in the Telugu epic of the battle of Palnadu around 1182.
velanati-chodas.e: Weakened by these wars, the Velanati Chodas were defeated in the early 13th century by the Kakatiya king Ganapati, who absorbed coastal Andhra into his kingdom around 1216.

vellavi.t: Gallic people of the Velay highlands around Le Puy, dependents of the Arverni.
vellavi.o: The Vellavi held the volcanic uplands of the upper Loire, in the modern Haute-Loire. Caesar lists them among the peoples under the authority of the [[s:arverni|Arverni]].
vellavi.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Their territory lay on the routes from the [[s:arverni|Arverni]] lands south towards the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]].
vellavi.e: They followed the [[s:arverni|Arverni]] into the revolt of 52 BCE. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] they formed a civitas with its chief town at Ruessium (Saint-Paulien), later moved to Anicium (Le Puy-en-Velay). Their name survives in the Velay.

vindhya-pradesh.t: The union of the Bundelkhand and Baghelkhand princely states, a short-lived Indian state with its capital at Rewa.
vindhya-pradesh.o: In 1948 the 35 states of the [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] and [[s:rewa-state|Baghelkhand]] agencies, among them Rewa, [[s:panna-state|Panna]], [[s:orchha-state|Orchha]], [[s:datia-state|Datia]] and many tiny estates, were merged into the United State of Vindhya Pradesh, with the Maharaja of Rewa, [[e:martand-singh|Martand Singh]], as Rajpramukh.
vindhya-pradesh.r: The union proved unstable, and in 1950 it was made a centrally administered Part C state, with some enclaves exchanged with Uttar Pradesh. It had a largely rural economy, many former princely estates and low literacy. Rewa served as capital, and [[s:datia-state|Datia]], [[s:orchha-state|Orchha]] and Khajuraho lay within its borders.
vindhya-pradesh.e: Under the States Reorganisation Act Vindhya Pradesh was merged into Madhya Pradesh on 1 November 1956.

voivodeship-of-litovoi.t: Romanian voivodeship west of the Olt whose ruler died fighting Hungary around 1279, an early step towards an independent Wallachia.
voivodeship-of-litovoi.o: Litovoi's land appears in Béla IV's charter of 1247 to the [[e:knights-hospitaller|Knights Hospitaller]], which names a knezate of Litovoi in the region of the Jiu and Olt, possibly including the Hațeg country across the Carpathians.
voivodeship-of-litovoi.r: Litovoi ruled Romanian knezes as a Hungarian tributary. A royal charter of 1285 says that around 1277–1279 a voivode Litovoi, with his brothers, seized part of the kingdom and refused to pay tribute to Ladislaus IV of [[e:hungary|Hungary]].
voivodeship-of-litovoi.e: A Hungarian force under Master George defeated the rebels: Litovoi was killed and his brother Bărbat captured and forced to pay a large ransom. The land later became part of the [[s:principality-of-wallachia|Principality of Wallachia]] under Basarab I.

venetian-monemvasia.t: Venetian rule over the rock fortress of Monemvasia, the last free Byzantine town in the Peloponnese and home of malmsey wine.
venetian-monemvasia.o: Monemvasia, a fortified town on a rock island off the Laconian coast, belonged to the [[s:despotate-of-the-morea|Despotate of the Morea]]. When [[e:mehmed-ii|Mehmed II]] conquered the Morea in 1460, the despot [[e:thomas-palaiologos|Thomas Palaiologos]] handed it to [[e:pope-pius-ii|Pope Pius II]]. Papal rule proved weak, and in 1464 the inhabitants placed themselves under [[e:venice|Venice]].
venetian-monemvasia.r: Venetian officials governed with the town's Greek notables, maintaining its fortifications and port. Monemvasia, called Malvasia by the Italians, gave its name to malmsey, a sweet wine traded across [[e:europe|Europe]], although by this time most of it came from [[e:crete|Crete]]. The town was largely cut off from its Ottoman-held hinterland.
venetian-monemvasia.e: In the peace of 1540 that ended the third Ottoman-Venetian war, [[e:venice|Venice]] ceded Monemvasia and Nauplia to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]]. It returned to Venetian control from 1690 to 1715 as part of the [[s:venetian-morea|Venetian Morea]].
